articles.title: Node.js Isn't Single-Threaded. How libuv and the OS Kernel Actually Run Your Code.
articles.description: A visual, 10-minute architectural deep dive into Node.js runtime internals. Learn how V8, the libuv threadpool, OS kernel event demultiplexers (epoll/kqueue/IOCP), the 6-phase event loop, and Worker Threads execute JavaScript under the hood.
articles.body_html:
Ask almost any software engineer how Node.js works, and you will hear the exact same sentence repeated like a universal law of physics:

"Node.js is single-threaded."

It is written in conference slides, repeated in job interviews, and taught in beginner bootcamps across the globe.

Yet if you start a basic Node.js HTTP server on a Linux machine and inspect the process with ps -eLf or htop, you will see something that immediately shatters that mental model:

Your single Node.js process is running eight or more native operating system threads simultaneously.

If Node.js were truly single-threaded:

  • Encrypting passwords with crypto.pbkdf2 would freeze your entire backend until the hash finished computing.
  • Reading a 4-gigabyte file from disk with fs.readFile would block every incoming HTTP request on your server.
  • Compressing response payloads with zlib would cause global latency spikes for all concurrent users.

None of those operations freeze your server.

The truth is that Node.js has never been a simple single-threaded program.

Node.js is a multi-threaded C and C++ runtime engine that presents a single-threaded JavaScript execution interface to developer code.

Underneath your JavaScript functions sits an intricate coordination machine powered by Google's V8 engine, the libuv cross-platform abstraction library, and operating system kernel primitives that have evolved over three decades.

To build fast, resilient, and non-blocking production backends, you have to look past the "single-threaded" slogan and understand how Node.js actually runs your code.

Here is what is really happening beneath your call stack.

The Three Tiers of Node.js: V8, libuv, and the Kernel

To see where the threads actually live, we need to decompose a Node.js process into its three distinct architectural layers.

[ Your JavaScript Code ]
          │
          ▼
[ Tier 1: Google V8 Engine ] ── Single-Threaded Call Stack & Heap
          │
          ▼
[ Tier 2: libuv Runtime ]   ── Event Loop + 4x Worker Threadpool
          │
          ▼
[ Tier 3: OS Kernel ]       ── Non-Blocking Sockets (epoll / kqueue / IOCP)

Tier 1: The JavaScript Execution Context (V8 Engine)

This is the only part of Node.js that is truly single-threaded.

Google's V8 engine executes your application code, user-defined functions, object allocations, and variable assignments within a single execution thread called the Main Thread.

Because the main thread executes one stack frame at a time, synchronous JavaScript loops (while (true) {}) or expensive recursive calculations will monopolize the CPU and starve the rest of your application.

Tier 2: The libuv Asynchronous Engine

When your JavaScript code calls an asynchronous Node.js API (such as reading a file, computing a hash, or resolving a domain name), V8 does not execute the underlying operating system call.

Instead, V8 passes the request across internal C++ bindings into libuv.

libuv is a high-performance C library originally built specifically for Node.js (and now also used by Julia and other languages).

libuv maintains two primary tools:

  1. The Event Loop: A single-threaded state machine that orchestrates callbacks and timers.
  2. The Worker Threadpool: A pool of pre-spawned background OS threads (defaulting to 4 threads) used to run blocking operations completely off the main thread.

Tier 3: The Operating System Kernel Subsystem

Here lies the biggest revelation in Node.js systems architecture:

Network I/O does not use the libuv worker threadpool at all.

When you create an HTTP server, connect to a PostgreSQL database, or open a WebSocket, your operating system kernel handles the network sockets through native event demultiplexers:

  • Linux: epoll
  • macOS and BSD: kqueue
  • Windows: IOCP (I/O Completion Ports)

These kernel subsystems monitor tens of thousands of network sockets concurrently without allocating a single OS thread.

File System I/O vs Network I/O: The Architectural Split

One of the most persistent misconceptions is that all asynchronous Node.js operations work the same way under the hood.

In reality, Node.js handles file system operations and network sockets through completely separate execution pipelines.

Why File I/O Requires Background Threads

Consider this common code:

import fs from 'node:fs';

fs.readFile('/var/log/app.log', (err, data) => {
  console.log('File read complete:', data.length);
});

Why does this asynchronous call require background threads?

Because across most operating systems (particularly Linux), there is no truly non-blocking API for regular disk file operations.

While network sockets can easily report whether incoming data is ready to be read, standard file systems on physical disk drives do not provide a universal, non-blocking asynchronous event interface.

If Node.js called read() on a disk file from the main V8 thread, and the hard drive heads had to seek across physical disk platters or wait for a network-mounted volume (NFS/EFS), the main thread would freeze for milliseconds. No HTTP requests could be handled during that pause.

To prevent this freeze:

  1. fs.readFile() packages the file descriptor and buffer into a work request (uv_work_t).
  2. libuv places the request into an internal task queue.
  3. An idle worker thread from the libuv threadpool picks up the request.
  4. The worker thread calls the blocking C system call read() entirely in the background.
  5. Once the bytes are read into memory, the worker thread posts a completion event back to the event loop.
  6. The main thread picks up the completion event during the Poll phase and invokes your JavaScript callback.

Why Network I/O Never Touches the Threadpool

Now look at an incoming HTTP request or an outgoing API fetch:

import http from 'node:http';

http.get('http://api.example.com/users', (res) => {
  res.on('data', (chunk) => {
    console.log('Received packet chunk');
  });
});

Does this operation take a thread from the libuv worker threadpool?

No. It consumes zero worker threads.

Network sockets are represented by file descriptors that support non-blocking mode. When Node.js creates a socket, it flags the socket as non-blocking:

// libuv sets O_NONBLOCK on socket file descriptors
fcntl(fd, F_SETFL, O_NONBLOCK);

Then, libuv registers the socket descriptor with the OS kernel's event demultiplexer (epoll_ctl on Linux).

The kernel's network stack monitors the physical Network Interface Card (NIC). When packets arrive over the wire, the hardware fires an interrupt, the kernel fills an internal buffer, and epoll marks the socket descriptor as readable.

libuv simply asks the kernel: "Which of our 20,000 registered sockets have data ready right now?"

The kernel returns the ready list instantly. Node.js reads the bytes and executes your callback, all without burning background worker threads.

This fundamental distinction explains why a single Node.js instance can easily hold 50,000 idle WebSocket connections open, yet simultaneously struggle if 10 threads attempt heavy cryptographic hashing at the same time.

The 6 Discrete Phases of the libuv Event Loop

Many developers picture the event loop as a basic JavaScript array of functions:

// The false mental model
while (queue.length > 0) {
  const callback = queue.shift();
  callback();
}

In the actual C implementation of libuv (src/unix/core.c), the event loop is a structured, six-phase state machine. Each phase maintains its own queue of pointers to C callbacks and operates on strict rules.

Here is what happens during each tick of the loop:

1. Timers Phase

The loop begins by checking for expired timers scheduled via setTimeout() and setInterval().

libuv stores active timers in a binary min-heap sorted by expiration timestamp. During this phase, libuv compares the current system clock with the root of the heap. It loops through all timers whose target time has arrived, executing their associated JavaScript callbacks in order.

2. Pending Callbacks (I/O Callbacks Phase)

This phase executes deferred system callbacks that were postponed from the previous loop iteration.

For instance, if a TCP socket connection attempt fails with an operating system error like ECONNREFUSED, some UNIX platforms report the error asynchronously. libuv defers reporting the error until this phase to give the system time to stabilize.

3. Idle / Prepare Phase

These two phases are used internally by libuv for housekeeping and synchronization before polling. Developer code cannot schedule callbacks directly into these queues.

4. Poll Phase: The Heart of Node.js

The Poll phase is where Node.js spends the vast majority of its operational life.

The Poll phase performs two critical responsibilities:

  1. It calculates how long it should block and wait for new I/O events.
  2. It processes ready events from the kernel demultiplexer (epoll_wait).

If the poll queue contains events (such as incoming network packets or completed file read operations from the threadpool), libuv iterates through them and executes their JavaScript callbacks synchronously.

What happens if the poll queue is empty?

  • If callbacks are scheduled in the setImmediate() queue (the Check phase), Node.js does not wait. It ends the Poll phase immediately and proceeds to Check.
  • If timers are pending in the Timers phase, libuv blocks only for the exact amount of time remaining until the earliest timer expires.
  • If no timers and no setImmediate calls are pending, libuv blocks indefinitely until the OS kernel signals that a network packet has arrived!

5. Check Phase (setImmediate)

The Check phase exists exclusively to execute callbacks registered via setImmediate().

Because the Check phase runs immediately after the Poll phase, setImmediate() callbacks are guaranteed to run right after incoming I/O events are processed, before the loop cycles back to check timers again.

6. Close Callbacks Phase

If a socket or stream is abruptly destroyed (such as socket.destroy() or socket.on('close')), its cleanup handler executes during this final phase, freeing allocated C structures before the next tick begins.

The Microtask Interceptors: process.nextTick vs Promises

Notice that neither process.nextTick() nor Promise.then() appeared in the six libuv phases above.

Why?

Because Microtasks are not part of the libuv event loop at all. They belong to the V8 engine layer.

Microtasks do not wait for the event loop to advance to a specific phase. Instead, they act as high-priority interceptors that run immediately after the current operation finishes, between every single callback, and at every phase boundary.

The Two Microtask Queues

Node.js manages two distinct microtask queues in memory:

  1. The process.nextTick Queue: Maintained internally by Node.js. It holds callbacks scheduled via process.nextTick().
  2. The Promise Microtask Queue: Maintained by the V8 engine. It holds resolved Promise callbacks (.then(), .catch(), await continuations, and queueMicrotask()).

The Strict Priority Ladder

Whenever the V8 JavaScript call stack empties:

  1. Node.js processes the nextTick queue until it is completely drained.
  2. Node.js processes the Promise microtask queue until it is completely drained.
  3. Only after both queues are empty does libuv resume executing the active phase of the event loop.

Consider this classic interview puzzle:

console.log("1: Synchronous");

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("2: setTimeout");
}, 0);

setImmediate(() => {
  console.log("3: setImmediate");
});

Promise.resolve().then(() => {
  console.log("4: Promise Microtask");
});

process.nextTick(() => {
  console.log("5: process.nextTick");
});

console.log("6: Synchronous End");

Here is the exact execution trace:

  1. console.log("1: Synchronous") executes on the call stack.
  2. setTimeout(..., 0) registers a timer in libuv's min-heap.
  3. setImmediate(...) queues a callback in libuv's Check phase queue.
  4. Promise.resolve().then(...) queues a callback in the V8 Promise microtask queue.
  5. process.nextTick(...) queues a callback in the nextTick queue.
  6. console.log("6: Synchronous End") executes on the call stack.
  7. The call stack is now empty. Before the event loop can proceed, the microtask interceptor runs:
    • It checks the nextTick queue: prints "5: process.nextTick".
    • It checks the Promise queue: prints "4: Promise Microtask".
  8. The event loop now begins. Depending on machine speed and process startup latency, the Timers phase or Check phase executes next, printing either 2 or 3.

The Starvation Hazard

Because process.nextTick drains completely before any event loop phase can continue, recursive nextTick calls will completely freeze your server:

function starveLoop() {
  process.nextTick(starveLoop); // Danger: Infinite recursion in microtask queue
}
starveLoop();

In this scenario, the Poll phase is never reached. Incoming HTTP requests, database responses, and file read operations are starved indefinitely. The server is completely paralyzed without throwing an error.

Threadpool Starvation: The Silent Performance Killer

Now let us examine what happens when developers run CPU-intensive tasks on Node.js without realizing they are sharing a tiny worker pool.

By default, the libuv threadpool size is set to 4 threads:

UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE = 4

These 4 threads are shared across:

  • All fs file system calls (fs.readFile, fs.writeFile, fs.stat)
  • Asynchronous cryptography (crypto.pbkdf2, crypto.scrypt, crypto.randomBytes)
  • Compression routines (zlib.gzip, zlib.brotliCompress)
  • DNS resolution via dns.lookup (which uses the blocking POSIX getaddrinfo() C library)

The Latency Spike Experiment

Imagine a Node.js authentication service that hashes passwords using crypto.pbkdf2:

import crypto from 'node:crypto';

function hashPassword(password) {
  const start = Date.now();
  crypto.pbkdf2(password, 'salt', 100_000, 64, 'sha512', () => {
    console.log(`Hash finished in ${Date.now() - start}ms`);
  });
}

// Five users attempt to log in at the exact same millisecond:
hashPassword('pass1');
hashPassword('pass2');
hashPassword('pass3');
hashPassword('pass4');
hashPassword('pass5');

If you run this code, you will observe an alarming result:

Hash finished in 82ms   // Request 1 (Thread 1)
Hash finished in 84ms   // Request 2 (Thread 2)
Hash finished in 85ms   // Request 3 (Thread 3)
Hash finished in 86ms   // Request 4 (Thread 4)
Hash finished in 168ms  // Request 5 (Queued!)

Requests 1 through 4 finish in roughly 84 milliseconds.

Request 5 takes twice as long (168 ms), even though all five requests do the exact same amount of work!

Why?

Because the threadpool only has 4 threads. Requests 1 through 4 monopolized every worker thread simultaneously. Request 5 sat completely frozen in the libuv task queue, waiting for one of the first four threads to finish before it could even begin computing.

Worse, while those 4 threads were computing hashes:

  • Any concurrent fs.readFile() on your server had to wait in the queue.
  • Any dns.lookup() domain resolution had to wait in the queue.
  • Your entire backend experienced sudden, mysterious latency spikes.

The Production Fix

You can increase the size of the worker threadpool up to 128 threads by setting the UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE environment variable:

UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=16 node server.js

Crucial Caveat: You must set this environment variable before the Node.js process starts. Setting process.env.UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE = 16 inside your JavaScript code will not work, because libuv initializes its threadpool during C startup before your script runs!

Modern Concurrency: Worker Threads & SharedArrayBuffer

Increasing UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE helps with I/O and native cryptography, but what if you need to run heavy JavaScript calculations (like parsing large JSON dumps, generating PDF reports, or running machine learning algorithms)?

JavaScript still executes on the single main V8 thread. Increasing the libuv threadpool will not help.

This is why Node.js introduced the worker_threads module.

Worker threads provide true CPU multi-threading inside Node.js by spinning up separate V8 instances on independent operating system threads.

Method 1: MessagePort & Structured Cloning

The standard way to communicate between worker threads is via parentPort.postMessage():

// main.js
import { Worker } from 'node:worker_threads';

const worker = new Worker('./heavy-task.js', {
  workerData: { items: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] }
});

worker.on('message', (result) => {
  console.log('Calculation complete:', result);
});

Under the hood, postMessage uses the HTML Structured Clone Algorithm.

It serializes the JavaScript object, copies the data across the thread boundary, and deserializes a fresh copy inside the worker thread's private memory heap.

This approach provides total memory isolation and zero risk of race conditions. However, if you pass a 500-megabyte dataset between threads, the serialization and copying overhead will consume substantial CPU time and memory.

Method 2: Zero-Copy Concurrency with SharedArrayBuffer & Atomics

For maximum performance, modern Node.js allows multiple worker threads to point directly to the exact same physical memory address using SharedArrayBuffer:

// main.js
import { Worker } from 'node:worker_threads';

// Allocate 1 kilobyte of shared physical RAM
const sharedBuffer = new SharedArrayBuffer(1024);
const sharedInts = new Int32Array(sharedBuffer);

const worker = new Worker('./worker.js', {
  workerData: { sharedBuffer }
});

// Wait for worker to signal update
Atomics.wait(sharedInts, 0, 0);
console.log('Worker updated index 0 to:', sharedInts[0]);

In the worker thread:

// worker.js
import { workerData } from 'node:worker_threads';

const sharedInts = new Int32Array(workerData.sharedBuffer);

// Mutate memory directly with atomic safety
Atomics.store(sharedInts, 0, 42);
Atomics.notify(sharedInts, 0, 1); // Wake up waiting main thread

With SharedArrayBuffer:

  • Zero data is copied or serialized.
  • Both the main thread and the worker thread read and write to the exact same RAM bytes.
  • The Atomics object provides thread-safe operations (load, store, add, wait, notify), preventing data races and corrupted memory states.

This transforms Node.js from a simple event-driven script runner into a high-concurrency systems platform capable of high-throughput numerical processing.

Architectural Takeaways for Production Backends

When you step back and look at the entire machine, the true architecture of Node.js becomes clear:

  1. JavaScript is single-threaded; Node.js is not. The V8 engine executes user code on a single thread, while libuv and the OS kernel handle concurrency with multiple native background threads.
  2. Network I/O is non-blocking at the kernel level. Sockets rely on epoll, kqueue, and IOCP, consuming zero worker threads and enabling immense network concurrency.
  3. File I/O and crypto rely on the libuv threadpool. A default pool of 4 threads means concurrent file reads or hashing operations can easily cause silent queuing bottlenecks.
  4. Microtasks take absolute priority. process.nextTick() and Promise callbacks run between every phase boundary. Recursive nextTicks will starve the event loop completely.
  5. Worker Threads unlock true CPU parallelism. For heavy CPU workloads, offload calculations to dedicated worker_threads using structured messaging or lock-free SharedArrayBuffer memory.

Node.js achieved its dominance not because single-threaded execution is inherently superior, but because its creators built a brilliant bridge between an intuitive, single-threaded developer model and the multi-threaded, asynchronous power of modern operating systems.

When you architect your next Node.js microservice or debug a mysterious production latency spike, which layer of the runtime usually causes the most surprises in your codebase? And how do you balance worker thread pools against external worker queues like Redis or BullMQ in your infrastructure?

References & Technical Standards:

  • libuv Official Architecture & Design Guide
  • Node.js Official Documentation: The Event Loop, Timers, and process.nextTick()
  • Node.js Core Repository: C++ libuv Integration & fs Implementation
  • Google V8 Engine Documentation: Memory Heap & Concurrency
  • POSIX Standards: Non-blocking I/O and epoll(7) Linux Programmer's Manual

articles.title: I Coded for 30 Days Using Only Claude Code — Here's What I Learned
articles.description: Not "AI-assisted." Not "copilot suggestions I edited." I made a rule: for 30 days I don't type...
articles.body_html:
Not "AI-assisted." Not "copilot suggestions I edited." I made a rule: for 30 days I don't type application code. The AI does. My job is to describe, review, and approve.

I shipped a real product this way — a small SaaS with auth, Stripe billing, a dashboard, and a public API. It works. It's in production. And along the way I found out exactly where the "AI writes everything now" dream holds up and where it quietly falls apart.

This isn't a hype post and it isn't a doom post. It's a field report.

The rules

To keep myself honest:

  1. I don't write application logic by hand. I prompt, the AI writes.
  2. I can read every line, reject it, and ask again — but I can't fix it myself in the editor.
  3. Config, secrets, and "click the button in the dashboard" steps are mine (the AI can't do those anyway).
  4. If I get truly stuck for more than an hour, I log it as a "break" and write the code myself.

By the end I had 9 logged breaks. Those breaks are the interesting part.

What worked shockingly well

Let me be fair to the machine first, because a lot of this genuinely surprised me.

Greenfield scaffolding is basically solved. "Set up a Next.js app with Postgres, Drizzle, and auth" — done, correctly, in one shot. The first 40% of the project flew by faster than I've ever built anything.

Boilerplate it never gets wrong. CRUD endpoints, form validation, Zod schemas, a table with sorting and pagination. The stuff I hate writing, produced perfectly, every time, no notes.

It's a phenomenal rubber duck. "Why is this query slow?" got me a better answer than I'd have reasoned to alone — it spotted a missing index and an N+1 in the same breath.

For the first week I genuinely thought I'd write the "developers are obsolete" post. Then week two happened.

What broke — the 9 breaks, honestly

Break 1–3: It can't hold the whole system in its head

Brilliant at the file in front of it, blind to the one three folders over. It wrote a second formatCurrency helper because it didn't know the first existed. Re-implemented my auth check inline instead of the middleware I already had. Introduced a subtly different User type in a new module.

None of these are "bugs" — everything compiled, everything passed. They're architecture drift, and architecture drift is invisible until the day it costs you a week.

The AI optimizes locally. Coherence across a system is still a human job.

Break 4–5: It confidently writes plausible, wrong code

The scariest failures weren't crashes. They were code that looked right and ran fine on the happy path.

The billing webhook it wrote acknowledged Stripe events before persisting them. Flawless in testing. In production, one DB blip = a paying customer locked out, no record, no trail. I only caught it because I've been burned by exactly this before. A junior copying this output would not have caught it. That's the part that keeps me up.

Break 6: Debugging its own code is a hall of mirrors

When something broke that the AI couldn't see, asking it to fix it produced changes, not fixes. It would rewrite the function, swear the bug was gone, and reintroduce it two prompts later. Without dropping into the debugger myself to understand the real state, we'd have spun forever. Biggest time sink of the month.

Break 7–8: Taste, and saying "no, less"

Asked for a settings page, it gave me 14 options nobody wanted. Asked for error handling, it wrapped everything in try/catch and swallowed the errors. The AI's instinct is always to add. Knowing what to leave out — the product-design part of engineering — it has none.

Break 9: The last 10% is still 90% of the work

"Demo works" took a week. "Handles a real user doing something weird at 2am" took the other three. Edge cases, race conditions, the empty state, the error state, the double-click state — the AI does none of it unless you know to ask, and knowing to ask is the job.

The uncomfortable synthesis

AI didn't replace me. It replaced the *tasks I used to give juniors.* The scaffolding, the boilerplate, the first draft — the exact work a junior becomes a senior by doing. So if the AI does all the entry-level work, where does the next senior come from? You can't skip the 10,000 hours; you can only move where they're spent.

The skills that mattered every single day were senior ones: knowing the code was subtly wrong, knowing what not to build, holding the whole system in my head to catch the drift. AI didn't flatten the hierarchy — it made the top more valuable and sawed off the ladder to get there.

What I actually changed

I didn't stop using AI — I use it for 100% of the typing now and always will. I changed the guardrails, and every one maps to a break above:

  • The thing that writes the code is never the thing that reviews it. A separate reviewer, prompted to refute the diff, catches the plausible-but-wrong code the author always waves through.
  • Nothing merges without a human who can see the blast radius the model can't.
  • "It compiles and the tests pass" is the start of review, not the end — the model writes tests that agree with its own wrong mental model.

Author here, skeptic there, human on the merge button — that separation is the whole reason I could hand the typing to a machine and still sleep. It's also exactly how we build xenition: agents that do the work, a different agent that tries to tear it down, and a person who owns the decision.

Would I do it again?

For a prototype? In a heartbeat — I'd never scaffold by hand again. For production? AI for 100% of the typing and 0% of the thinking. The typing was never the hard part. It just felt like it was.

articles.title: You're Debouncing Scroll Wrong. requestAnimationFrame Fixes It.
articles.description: Debouncing a scroll handler makes it wait until scrolling stops — which is why your sticky header always lags half a beat. requestAnimationFrame fixes the lag by syncing updates to the browser's own paint clock instead of a timer.
articles.body_html:
Our sticky header started lagging behind the scroll by about half a second. Not broken — just late, like it was watching the page over a bad video call. Scroll up fast and the header's drop shadow would still be fading in a beat after you'd already stopped.

The code looked right. It was debounced, just like the resize handler two files over, just like every "optimize this event listener" article says to do. Debouncing a scroll handler is the move everyone learns for performance reasons. Nobody mentions it also breaks the thing you were trying to show the user in real time.

The handler that was "optimized" into being wrong

Here's roughly what was wrapping the scroll listener:

function debounce(fn, wait) {
  let timer;
  return (...args) => {
    clearTimeout(timer);
    timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), wait);
  };
}

window.addEventListener("scroll", debounce(updateHeader, 150));

debounce resets its timer on every single scroll event and only fires once the events stop coming — once you stop scrolling. That's exactly what you want for a resize handler recalculating a layout: you don't care about every intermediate width, just the final one, and recalculating 40 times mid-drag is wasted work.

A sticky header isn't that. The user wants to see the shadow and background opacity change as they scroll, not 150ms after they've already arrived. Debounce doesn't throttle the rate of updates — it delays the update until the interaction is over. For anything the user is supposed to watch happen live, that's backwards.

Quick gut check before you keep reading: have you ever debounced a scroll or mousemove handler because that's just "what you do" for frequent events, without asking whether debounce or throttle was the one you actually needed?

Throttling fixes the lag. It doesn't fix the timing.

The standard next move is to swap debounce for throttle — run the handler on a fixed interval instead of waiting for silence:

function throttle(fn, wait) {
  let last = 0;
  return (...args) => {
    const now = Date.now();
    if (now - last >= wait) {
      last = now;
      fn(...args);
    }
  };
}

window.addEventListener("scroll", throttle(updateHeader, 16));

This is closer — the header updates during the scroll now. But look at that 16. Where did it come from? It's "roughly one frame at 60Hz," typed in because that's the number every blog post uses. It assumes the display is 60Hz. A lot of phones and newer monitors run at 90Hz, 120Hz, even 144Hz — on those, 16 isn't "once per frame" anymore, it's "slower than the screen can actually paint," and the update looks subtly behind even though your throttle is technically running.

You're also still paying for a Date.now() call and a comparison on every scroll event, even the ones you throw away. The scroll event itself can fire dozens of times between two paints. All of that extra firing is wasted — the browser is only going to show the user a new frame once, no matter how many times you ran your handler before it.

The browser already has a clock for this

Here's the part that's easy to miss: the browser knows exactly when it's about to paint the next frame. You don't have to estimate it with a setTimeout interval — you can ask for it directly with requestAnimationFrame.

let ticking = false;

function onScroll() {
  if (ticking) return;
  ticking = true;
  requestAnimationFrame(() => {
    updateHeader();
    ticking = false;
  });
}

window.addEventListener("scroll", onScroll, { passive: true });

The ticking flag is the whole trick. scroll can fire many times before the next paint; the flag makes sure only the first one of those schedules an update, and every scroll event after it until the next frame is a no-op — a single boolean check, nothing more. When the browser is finally ready to paint, it calls your callback once, you update the header with the latest scroll position, and you flip the flag back so the next scroll event can schedule the next frame.

No guessed interval. No wasted setTimeout calls that get cleared before they fire. No lag after the user stops, because there's no waiting-for-silence step at all — the update rides along with the very next frame the browser was already going to paint, on a 60Hz screen or a 120Hz one.

{ passive: true } is still worth keeping on the listener, but be precise about why: scroll itself isn't cancelable, so preventDefault() inside a scroll handler does nothing either way — passive or not. The option earns its keep on events that are cancelable, like touchmove and wheel, where it tells the browser you'll never call preventDefault() so it can start scrolling immediately instead of waiting to find out. Add it to the scroll listener anyway as the correct default for any handler that never cancels anything.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

When you still want debounce

None of this makes debounce wrong in general — it just means the choice depends on what the user is waiting for. A search-as-you-type box should wait for the person to stop typing. A "save draft" call should wait for a pause in edits. A window-resize recalculation that's expensive should wait until the user's done dragging the edge of the browser.

The question that decides it: does the user need to see this update during the interaction, or only after it settles? Live visual feedback — scroll position, drag position, pointer tracking — wants a per-frame throttle, and requestAnimationFrame is the native, interval-free way to get one. Anything that's expensive and only matters at the end wants debounce.

The header stopped lagging the day we swapped the setTimeout number for a question the browser could just answer itself.

articles.title: Bookmark Buddy: Gemma Tidies Your Messy Bookmarks While You Put Your Feet Up
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady          ...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

My bookmarks bar is a mess. I have years and years worth of bookmarks that I hadn't looked through in so long - 722 to be exact. Cleaning it up is the kind of chore I'll put off forever.

So I built Bookmark Buddy 🦥, a Chrome and Edge extension that tidies your real bookmarks for you, then keeps them tidy.

Introducing Mochi, the sloth that does the tidying!

  • Reads your bookmarks right in the browser. No exporting.
  • Finds duplicates on its own, even when the links differ by http vs https, a trailing slash, or tracking codes like utm_source
  • Suggests 6–9 folders that fit your bookmarks, which you can rename, remove or add to. Already have folders you like? Keep my folders keeps them (subfolders too) and only sorts the loose bookmarks.
  • Handles subfolders. Add your own, or have Gemma split a big folder into a few subfolders (Recipes › Dinners, Desserts)
  • Sorts every bookmark into those folders, slow and steady, a few at a time
  • Lets you fix anything: drag bookmarks between folders or into a new order, rename, add or reorder folders, and delete what you don't need
  • Applies it in one click. Your bookmarks move into the new folders and the empty old ones are cleared out. A backup is saved first, so Undo everything puts it all back.
  • Sorts new bookmarks as you save them. Drop a bookmark in your Bookmarks bar and Mochi files it, with a little notification and an Undo button.

There's also a web version that works in any WebGPU browser: drop in a bookmarks export and download a clean file to import back.

The sorting is done by Gemma, running entirely in your browser. Your bookmarks never leave your device.

Who gets to be lazier: anyone whose bookmarks bar has turned into a junk drawer, which is pretty much everyone. And once it's clean, you never have to clean it again.

Demo

Try the extension (Chrome or Edge):

  1. Download bookmark-buddy-extension.zip from the latest release and unzip it.
  2. Go to chrome://extensions (or edge://extensions), turn on Developer mode, click Load unpacked, and pick the unzipped folder.
  3. Click Mochi 🦥 in your toolbar.

Coming soon to the Chrome Web Store and Edge Add-ons, so it'll be a one-click install.

Try the web version: https://bookmark-buddy.onrender.com (Chrome or Edge on a laptop works best. Click "Try it with sample bookmarks" if you don't want to use your own.)

Code

tmott13 / bookmark-buddy

🦥 Tidies your messy bookmarks with Gemma running on your device, then sorts new ones as you save them. A Chrome/Edge extension plus a web app. Nothing is uploaded, and you can undo everything.

🦥 Bookmark Buddy

Your messy bookmarks, tidied while you put your feet up. Meet Mochi, the sloth who does the tidying 🦥🍡

Bookmark Buddy sorts your bookmarks into clean folders, catches duplicates, and keeps everything tidy as you save new ones. The sorting is done by Gemma running in your browser with WebLLM, so your bookmarks (your bank, your job search, your health sites…) never leave your device.

It comes two ways:

  • 🧩 Chrome / Edge extension (the lazy way): tidies your real bookmarks in place, with one-click Undo everything, then sorts new bookmarks automatically as you save them.
  • 🌐 Web app: bookmark-buddy.onrender.com. Works in any WebGPU browser. Drop in a bookmarks export and download a tidy file to import back.

Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 3: Slow and Steady.

Install the extension

  1. Download bookmark-buddy-extension.zip from the latest release and unzip it.
  2. Go…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

  • Open model: Gemma 2 2B (gemma-2-2b-it-q4f16_1-MLC) on laptops, with Gemma 3 1B as the lighter option for phones.
  • Runs in the browser: WebLLM runs Gemma on your GPU with WebGPU. The model downloads once and is cached, so it even works offline.
  • Frontend: Angular 22 with signals. Your session is saved in your browser, so a refresh doesn't lose your progress.
  • Extension: Manifest V3. The same Angular app is the extension's page. A small background worker listens for new bookmarks, and when one needs a folder it opens a hidden offscreen page that runs Gemma on the GPU, then closes it a few minutes later to give the memory back.
  • Hosting: a free static site on Render, with no backend at all.

Like my last two projects, the big idea is Gemma makes the judgment calls, and the app keeps your data safe:

  1. Gemma never touches a URL. It only sees each bookmark's title and website, and replies with a folder name. The app copies the actual links, dates and icons, so nothing can get mangled.
  2. Nothing gets deleted unless you say so. Duplicates and old dev links go into a "Maybe delete?" folder with a reason, so you decide. You can delete anything with one click (or clear out the whole "Maybe delete?" folder), and restore it until you apply. The extension saves a backup first and can undo everything.
  3. Nothing gets lost. If Gemma skips a bookmark or makes up a folder name, the app catches it and puts it in "Other." Every bookmark you keep ends up in a folder.
  4. Small batches, with examples. A 2B model does much better sorting 6 bookmarks than 300, so it works through them in small batches, slow and steady, like a sloth. Each batch also shows Gemma a few bookmarks it already sorted, so similar pages land in the same folder.
  5. The app handles the obvious ones. If a title or site clearly names a folder ("Easy taco recipe" → Recipes), the app files it without asking Gemma. Gemma only gets the judgment calls.
  6. It learns as it goes. Once Gemma puts the same site in the same folder twice, the rest of that site's bookmarks follow automatically, which saves time. Sites with every kind of content, like YouTube and Reddit, always get a fresh look. When you save a bookmark into a folder yourself, or hit Undo on a guess, Mochi learns from that too.
  7. It never blocks you. If Gemma isn't downloaded yet, a new bookmark waits in a "Needs a home" folder until you open Bookmark Buddy, instead of getting lost.

I was surprised by how well Gemma worked to generate the proper folder names for my bookmarks. I also loved how fast Mochi worked to organize all of my bookmarks.

My first version didn’t get it right. Gemma sorted 12 bookmarks at a time, and my recipes ended up scattered across a few different folders. The fix was slowing it down: 6 bookmarks at a time, plus a few already-sorted examples so Gemma stays consistent. Turns out slow and steady really does win, just like Mochi.

I built this with Claude as my pair programmer. I picked the problem, made the product calls, and tested it on my own bookmarks.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • Bookmarks are personal. They show your bank, your job search, your health sites, your hobbies. With an open model running on your own device, none of that gets uploaded to anyone's server.
  • It's free to run. No API bill, no subscription. Set it up once, tidy whenever you want.
  • It works offline. Once Gemma is downloaded, you can tidy your bookmarks on a plane.
  • I control the whole pipeline. I decide what the model sees (titles, not URLs), how it's batched, and the safety rules around it. A closed API would be a black box in the middle of my bookmarks.

The Lazy Payoff

I was able to organize all 722 of my bookmarks! I also kept my folders, which I loved.

It took me about 15 minutes in total to organize my bookmarks. I had about 40 bookmarks that Mochi put into an "Other" folder that I went through line by line to sort. The app did everything I needed it to do. I love that I could drag n drop bookmarks, create new folders, and delete bookmarks, all in one place! This app saved me so much time and it was very low effort. Perfect for a lazy sloth like myself.

What's Next: Bookmark Buddy 1.1.0

  • Chrome Web Store and Edge Add-ons: a one-click install with automatic updates, no Developer mode needed
  • Right-click "Ask Mochi to file this": sort any bookmark on demand, including old ones sitting in the wrong folder
  • A weekly tidy-up: a gentle nudge like "Mochi found 4 bookmarks that could use a home," then one click to review
  • A toolbar popup: see what's waiting in "Needs a home" and turn auto-sorting on or off without opening a full tab
  • A first-run welcome: a quick tour of what Mochi does and help picking a Gemma model

What should Mochi learn next? Tell me in the comments 🦥

Prize Categories

  • Gemma: Gemma 2 2B and Gemma 3 1B run fully in the browser with WebLLM, suggesting folders, sorting every bookmark, and filing new ones in the background.
  • Render: the web version is deployed as a free Render static site from a render.yaml blueprint.

Thanks to DEV, the Hacktoberfest team, and the MLC/WebLLM and Gemma teams. And a belated Happy International Sloth Day (Oct 20) from Mochi! 🦥

articles.title: My Reducer's Switch Stopped Being Exhaustive. `as const` Fixed It.
articles.description: Object and array literals widen to `string` and `number` the moment you write them, which quietly breaks discriminated unions and exhaustive switch checks. `as const` keeps the literal types — but it also freezes the value, which bites in its own way.
articles.body_html:
The PR review catches it at the worst possible moment — the day after it shipped. A teammate added a 'reset' action to the cart reducer, ran the tests, watched them pass, and merged. The switch statement never ran the new branch. Not an error. Not a warning. The build was green the whole time.

Here's the reducer, trimmed down to the shape that matters:

function cartReducer(state: CartState, action: { type: string; payload?: unknown }) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'add':
      return { ...state, items: [...state.items, action.payload] };
    case 'remove':
      return { ...state, items: state.items.filter((i) => i.id !== action.payload) };
    // 'reset' was added here as an afterthought, then deleted by accident
    // during a rebase. TypeScript never noticed either way.
  }
  return state;
}

action.type is typed as string. TypeScript can check a switch against a union of specific values and tell you when a case is missing. It cannot check a switch against all possible strings — there's no way to be "exhaustive" over an infinite type. So the compiler does the only honest thing: it says nothing.

The bug wasn't the missing case. The bug was string — and it was there before anyone touched the reducer.

Where the type actually came from

Nobody typed action.type: string on purpose. It came from the action creators:

function reset() {
  return { type: 'reset' };
}

reset(); // return type: { type: string }

That's the part that surprises people. reset is a const-worthy, never-reassigned function returning a single literal. You'd expect { type: 'reset' } to stay exactly that specific. It doesn't — and the reason is really about mutability, not constants.

const status = 'idle';
// type: 'idle' — status can never change, so TypeScript keeps the literal

const config = { status: 'idle' };
// config.status type: string — config.status CAN be reassigned
// (config.status = 'loading' compiles fine), so TypeScript widens
// the property to the general type that covers anything you might assign

A const binding to a primitive can't be reassigned, so TypeScript has no reason to generalize — the literal type is the only thing it will ever hold. A property inside an object is a different story: config is const, but config.status isn't. TypeScript widens object and array members to their general type — string, number, boolean — because it's inferring a type that has to tolerate future writes, not just describe the value in front of it. Same rule for arrays:

const methods = ['GET', 'POST'];
// type: string[] — any string could get pushed in later

That widening is usually what you want. It's only a problem when the whole point of the value was to be one of a fixed, known set — an action's type, a theme name, an HTTP method you're about to switch on.

Before you scroll — what do you think turns string back into the literal 'idle'?

as const tells TypeScript to stop generalizing

as const is a type assertion that does the opposite of widening: it takes the literal, narrowest type of exactly what you wrote, and makes every property (recursively) readonly so there's no future write to protect against.

const config = { status: 'idle' } as const;
// config.status type: 'idle'  (readonly)

const methods = ['GET', 'POST'] as const;
// type: readonly ['GET', 'POST']  — a fixed-length, literal tuple, not string[]

Apply it to the action creators and the whole chain fixes itself:

function reset() {
  return { type: 'reset' } as const;
}
function add(payload: Item) {
  return { type: 'add', payload } as const;
}
function remove(id: string) {
  return { type: 'remove', payload: id } as const;
}

type CartAction = ReturnType<typeof reset> | ReturnType<typeof add> | ReturnType<typeof remove>;
// { type: 'reset' } | { type: 'add'; payload: Item } | { type: 'remove'; payload: string }

action.type inside the reducer is now 'add' | 'remove' | 'reset' instead of string — a real, finite union. Switch over it, and TypeScript can finally do the one thing it couldn't before:

function cartReducer(state: CartState, action: CartAction): CartState {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'add':
      return { ...state, items: [...state.items, action.payload] };
    case 'remove':
      return { ...state, items: state.items.filter((i) => i.id !== action.payload) };
    default:
      return assertNever(action); // ← now a compile error if a case is missing
  }
}

function assertNever(x: never): never {
  throw new Error(`Unhandled action: ${JSON.stringify(x)}`);
}

Delete the 'reset' case and action reaching the default branch is no longer never — it's { type: 'reset' }, which doesn't satisfy assertNever's never parameter. TypeScript flags it at the call site, at compile time, before a reviewer has to catch it by reading carefully. That's the whole fix: one three-letter suffix, in the three functions that build the actions.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

The part that bites back

Here's where it gets uglier, and where most explanations of as const stop too early. as const didn't just lock in the literal type — it made the value readonly, all the way down. That's not a side effect you can opt out of; it's the mechanism.

const METHODS = ['GET', 'POST'] as const;

METHODS.push('PUT');
// Error: Property 'push' does not exist on type 'readonly ["GET", "POST"]'

A readonly tuple has no mutating methods at all — no push, pop, splice, or index assignment. That's usually fine; you reached for as const because you wanted a fixed set, not a growable list. But it surfaces somewhere you won't expect the first time:

function logAllowedMethods(methods: string[]) {
  console.log(methods.join(', '));
}

logAllowedMethods(METHODS);
// Error: Argument of type 'readonly ["GET", "POST"]' is not assignable
// to parameter of type 'string[]'. The type 'readonly ["GET", "POST"]'
// is 'readonly' and cannot be assigned to the mutable type 'string[]'.

logAllowedMethods never mutates its argument, but its signature promises TypeScript it's allowed to. TypeScript can't verify that promise against a value it knows is frozen, so it refuses the call outright — correctly, because somewhere else methods.push(...) really would be legal against that same signature. Two ways out, and they mean different things:

function logAllowedMethods(methods: readonly string[]) { /* ... */ }
logAllowedMethods(METHODS); // fine — the parameter now admits it won't mutate

// or, if the function genuinely can't change:
logAllowedMethods([...METHODS]); // fine — a fresh, mutable copy

Widen the parameter if the function is well-behaved and just reads. Copy the array if you don't control the function. Either is one line; the trap is not knowing which bug you're looking at when the red squiggle shows up two files away from the as const that caused it.

Where it's worth reaching for

  • Action/event objects — reducers, event buses, anywhere a type or kind field drives a switch. This is the highest-leverage use; it's the difference between a real exhaustiveness check and a decorative one.
  • Fixed option lists — const THEMES = ['light', 'dark', 'system'] as const; then type Theme = (typeof THEMES)[number]; gives you the union 'light' | 'dark' | 'system' for free, generated from the one array you'll actually iterate to build a <select>.
  • Enum-free constant maps — const Role = { ADMIN: 'admin', EDITOR: 'editor' } as const; reads better than a TypeScript enum for most teams and gives you (typeof Role)[keyof typeof Role] as the type.
  • Not for values you're going to mutate. If you need to .push() into it later, as const is actively the wrong tool — reach for an explicit type annotation instead.

And if you're already validating the shape against an interface, you may not need as const at all — satisfies checks a value against a type and keeps its inferred literals, in one step, without the readonly. The two solve overlapping problems from opposite directions: as const narrows by removing information you didn't ask TypeScript to track (mutability); satisfies narrows by not throwing away information you already had. Worth knowing both before reaching for either.

The missing 'reset' case made it to production because string doesn't have gaps to find. as const is how you tell TypeScript the value in front of it is the only value it will ever be — so when you miss one, the compiler misses it too, loudly, before a reviewer has to.

Where has a widened type let a real bug through for you — and did you reach for as const, or something else?

articles.title: Is Open Source Still Open? A Look at Recent License Changes and Who They Hurt
articles.description: A few years ago, I checked a dependency’s license once, at install time, and never again. That habit...
articles.body_html:
A few years ago, I checked a dependency’s license once, at install time, and never again. That habit is getting expensive.

License changes aren’t new, but they’re happening often enough that “it’s open source” is no longer a permanent property of a project. It’s a status that can change between releases.

The pattern is almost always the same.

The shift nearly always runs one way: from an OSI-approved permissive or copyleft license toward a “source-available” license the Open Source Initiative doesn’t recognize as open source.

The Business Source License (BSL) is the most common destination. It’s a “delayed open source” license: the vendor sets restrictions up front, and each version converts to a true open-source license after a change date, typically four years out.

It’s not just the famous cases anymore. A few from this year alone:

  • Loki Mode moved from the MIT License to BSL 1.1 effective March 19, 2026.
  • Unleash announced in June 2026 that its core repository is moving from Apache 2.0 to AGPLv3. AGPL is OSI-approved, so this one is a different kind of change, but it still affects anyone embedding the code.
  • MiniMax moved its M2.7 AI model from MIT to a non-commercial license, which drew immediate backlash.

Who it actually hurts

  • 1. Small teams and agencies building on top: If your product depends on a library that relicenses, you now have three options: pay, migrate, or fork. Big companies have legal teams for that. A five-person shop usually doesn’t.
  • 2. Contributors: People gave their time to a project under one set of terms. When the company controlling it changes the rules, the community’s work becomes part of a product they no longer fully share in.
  • 3. Downstream projects: Plugins, integrations, and tutorials built around a tool inherit the uncertainty when its license shifts.

The fair counterargument

I don’t think vendors are simply villains here. Many of these changes were a response to cloud providers selling managed versions of a project without funding it. Maintainers need a sustainable model, and “be open and hope for donations” has a poor track record.

It’s also not always one-way. Redis is back under a recognized open-source license for those who choose it, while Valkey continues to be actively developed. Competition between the original and the fork may have pushed both toward better outcomes. Broader data also suggests permissive licensing has been rising, so this isn’t a total collapse of open source.

What I do now

  • Check who controls the project A single company controlling a project can relicense future versions at any time, while a project run by a neutral foundation with many contributing companies is much harder to change.
  • Read the license on every major upgrade, not just at install.
  • Pin versions so a surprise change doesn’t land in your next deploy.
  • Know your exit. Is there a credible fork? A foundation-backed alternative?
  • Set up license-change alerts for your critical dependencies.

So, is open source still open?

My honest answer: the code is still often open. The guarantee isn’t. Open source has always depended on trust, and trust now needs a little due diligence.

Over to you: Has a license change ever forced your team to migrate? Do you think relicensing is a fair business move, or a betrayal of the community that built the project? Tell me in the comments.

articles.title: How EU shops label the 30-day lowest price, and how a browser extension reads them in 15 languages
articles.description: Since 2022 every shop in the EU that advertises a price reduction has to show the lowest price it...
articles.body_html:
Since 2022 every shop in the EU that advertises a price reduction has to show the lowest price it charged in the 30 days before the reduction. That is Article 6a of the Price Indication Directive, added by the Omnibus Directive 2019/2161. The rule is the same everywhere. The way shops print it is not.

I maintain truediscount, a free, open source extension for Chrome and Firefox that puts a small badge on product pages and tells you whether a discount is real. This post is about the messiest part of that job: finding the 30-day price on a page, in whatever language and layout the shop chose.

What the label looks like across countries

A few real phrasings, collected from shop pages:

Country Typical label
Germany, Austria Niedrigster Preis der letzten 30 Tage: 49,99 €
France Prix le plus bas des 30 derniers jours : 49,99 €
Italy Prezzo più basso degli ultimi 30 giorni: 49,99 €
Spain Precio más bajo de los últimos 30 días: 49,99 €
Netherlands, Belgium Laagste prijs van de afgelopen 30 dagen: € 49,99
Poland Najniższa cena z 30 dni przed obniżką: 49,99 zł
Czechia Nejnižší cena za posledních 30 dní: 1 299 Kč
Romania Cel mai mic preț din ultimele 30 de zile: 249,99 lei
Sweden Lägsta pris senaste 30 dagarna: 499 kr

On top of the language there are layout differences:

  1. Inline label. The number sits in the same short element as the words. This is the easy case.
  2. Footnote. The struck price carries an asterisk and the explanation lives in the page footer, far away from the number. About You does this with "Letzter niedrigster Preis: der letzten 30 Tage vor der Preisermäßigung".
  3. Tooltip or popover. Alternate puts the explanation in a popover attribute on an info icon next to the price.
  4. Nothing at all next to the struck price. The crossed out number is the shop's own earlier price and you have to trust that it is the 30-day low.
  5. RRP instead. The struck price is the manufacturer's recommended price ("UVP" in German, "PVPR" in Spanish, "adviesprijs" in Dutch). Comparing against RRP is legal, but it says nothing about what the shop charged last month.

Case 5 matters most for shoppers, because "was 599, now 349" reads like a 42% cut when it is really a cut against a list price nobody paid.

How the extension reads it

The extractor runs in three passes, all on the page that is already open. Nothing is crawled and nothing leaves the browser.

Pass 1: the current price. Structured data first (JSON-LD Product and Offer, including products nested inside other types, then microdata), then a per shop selector if one exists, then generic selectors.

Pass 2: the advertised old price. Per shop selectors first, then generic ones such as s, del, [style*="line-through"] and class names containing old-price or strike. A candidate only counts if it is higher than the current price and less than 20 times it, which filters out unrelated numbers.

The kind of old price is decided by its label. The newest fix (v0.9.0) came from Lidl, which renders UVP: <s>599.00</s>. The word sits in the parent element, not inside the <s>, so the extension now also looks at the short parent text:

const label = (el.parentElement?.textContent || '').length < 60 ? el.parentElement.textContent : '';
oldKind = /rrp|uvp|retail price|adviesprijs|\bmsrp\b/i.test(`${selector} ${el.textContent} ${label} ${hint}`)
  ? 'rrp' : 'previous';

On lidl.fr the same layout shows a bare <s>49.99 €</s> with no label, and that stays a "previous price".

Pass 3: the shop's own 30-day disclosure. Two regular expressions do most of the work (shortened here): one for "lowest" in about 15 languages and one for "30 days":

const LOW_WORD = /(lowest|niedrigste|tiefstpreis|le plus bas|più basso|más bajo|laagste|najniższa|nejnižší|cel mai mic|lägsta|laveste|alhaisin|legalacsonyabb|najniža)/iu;
const DAYS_30 = /30[\s\u00a0-]*(?:tage?n?|days?|jours|giorni|días|dagen|dagarna|dni|dní|zile|dana|nap)/giu;

When both match inside a short element, the first price in that element becomes the shop's declared 30-day low. Prices are parsed with EU formats in mind: 1.299,99 €, 1 299 Kč, 49,- and € 49,99 all come out as numbers.

The verdict

With those three numbers the badge says one of a few things:

  • The old price matches the shop's 30-day low: the discount is real.
  • The old price is higher than the declared 30-day low: the discount is inflated, and the badge shows the real percentage.
  • The old price is an RRP: the badge says so and shows the 30-day low if the shop printed one.
  • No disclosure on the page: the extension falls back to its own local price history (one price per day, kept 90 days on your device).

What is still hard

  • Footnote layouts (case 2) are only understood when the footnote is close to the price. Matching asterisks across a whole page gives too many false hits.
  • Many shops render prices with JavaScript after load, so the content script watches the page for changes and checks again once it settles.
  • Several big shops block automated requests, so I can only build per shop rules from pages I can actually load. The supported shops page says which shops are tested against live pages and which only use generic rules.

If a shop near you prints the 30-day label in a way the extension misses, the popup has a "Report a problem" button that opens a prefilled GitHub issue with just the domain. That is the fastest way to get a new country covered before Black Friday. And if the badge gets in the way on a site you do not care about, v0.10.0 lets you hide it per domain from the popup; nothing is recorded on hidden sites.

This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

SlothSort is a privacy-first, local AI file organizer that turns your chaotic Downloads folder into a structured workspace. It scans your digital clutter, uses local AI to classify each file, and presents a neat organization plan. You simply review the proposed folders and click "Approve"—letting you reclaim your time and embrace your inner sloth without compromising your data.

Demo

Project will run on localhost and does not have a .com link

Code

shrguhaneogi-pixel / SlothSort 

        .-""""-
       /  .--.  \      🦥  slow sorting, steady results
      /  /    \  \
      | | 0  0 | |      [ messy files ]  ->  [ calm folders ]
      | |  __  | |
       \ \____/ /
        '.___.'
          /|\

SlothSort

articles.title: Vue v-for: The Directive Unmounted Hook Bug, Fixed in 3.5.41
articles.description: A custom directive's unmounted hook could silently skip firing inside a keyed v-for list. The directive unmounted hook bug, Vue's real fix, and a cheat sheet.
articles.body_html:
You write a custom directive once — v-tooltip, v-click-outside, v-ripple — attach something in mounted(), tear it down in unmounted(), and trust the pair like you'd trust addEventListener/removeEventListener. Then you drop it onto a row inside a filterable v-for list. Filter an item out. No error. No warning. The row disappears from the screen — and on some Vue 3 versions, unmounted() never ran. The listener it attached is still live, attached to a DOM node nothing references anymore. This was a real bug in Vue's own compiler, open for years, fixed only in Vue 3.5.41 — and understanding why it happened teaches you more about how v-for actually works than the fix note ever will.

What You'll Learn

By the end of this article you'll be able to:

  • Explain why a custom directive's lifecycle hooks can be skipped for an element inside v-for, even though the same directive works fine outside a loop
  • Reproduce the symptom, confirm whether your installed Vue version is affected, and verify the fix
  • Describe what a compiler patch flag is and why NEED_PATCH specifically matters for refs, vnode hooks, and custom directives
  • Write directive-based cleanup you can trust inside a list, instead of discovering the gap in production
  • Tell this bug apart from unrelated v-for gotchas (duplicate keys, index-as-key) that look similar but have different causes

Who this is for: you've written a custom directive with app.directive() or a local directives option, and you've used v-for with :key. If directives themselves are new to you, the Vue Guide to Custom Directives is worth reading first — this article assumes you know what mounted/unmounted hooks are, not how to write your first one.

Table of Contents

  • The Problem: A Cleanup Hook That Sometimes Doesn't Run
  • The Mental Model: Patch Flags Decide What the Runtime Bothers to Visit
  • The Bug, the Issue, and the Fix
  • Edge Cases and Gotchas
  • Best Practices
  • FAQ
  • Cheat Sheet
  • Key Takeaways

This is written against Vue 3.5.x (verified 3.5.43, current on npm's latest tag as of this writing). Vue 3.6 is still a release candidate (3.6.0-rc.10 on the rc tag) and isn't stable yet, so nothing here depends on it. The fix this article covers shipped in Vue 3.5.41, released August 5, 2026 — if your package.json pins anything older, you are likely affected (one of the two issues the fix closed was filed against 3.2.47, so this isn't a 3.5-only gap).

The Problem: A Cleanup Hook That Sometimes Doesn't Run

Say you've written a small directive that logs its own lifecycle — a stand-in for anything real a directive might do (attach a listener, instantiate a third-party widget, start an observer):

<!-- the directive — nothing unusual about it -->
<script setup>
const vLog = {
  mounted(el, binding) {
    console.log(`mounted: row ${binding.value}`)
  },
  unmounted(el, binding) {
    console.log(`unmounted: row ${binding.value}`)
    // in real code: removeEventListener, destroy a tooltip instance,
    // disconnect an observer — whatever mounted() set up
  },
}
</script>

Used on a single element, it behaves exactly as documented: one mounted log when it appears, one unmounted log when it's removed. Now put the same directive on an element inside a keyed v-for, and remove an item from the middle of the list by filtering the underlying array:

<template>
  <div v-for="row in visibleRows" :key="row.id" v-log="row.id">
    {{ row.label }}
  </div>
</template>

// remove row 2 from the data the list is built from
visibleRows.value = visibleRows.value.filter(r => r.id !== 2)

On an affected Vue version, row 2's <div> disappears from the DOM exactly as expected — but the console only ever shows the mounted log for it, never unmounted. Nothing throws. Nothing warns. The directive's cleanup code simply never executes for that element, while the identical directive on a non-looped element works every time. That asymmetry — directive hooks are reliable alone, unreliable in a v-for — is the entire bug, and it's what makes it so easy to ship without noticing: your manual test on one element passes, and the loop case only misbehaves once a list gets edited in production.

The Mental Model: Patch Flags Decide What the Runtime Bothers to Visit

The mental model: at compile time, Vue's template compiler inspects every element and decides which ones are worth revisiting when the component re-renders. An element with no dynamic text, no bound class, no bound prop — nothing that could ever change — gets compiled as fully static, and the runtime skips it entirely on every future patch. That skip is most of why Vue is fast: it never diffs what it already knows can't change.

To make that work, the compiler attaches a patch flag to every dynamic element — a small integer bitmask recording which kind of dynamic content it has: TEXT for interpolated text, CLASS/STYLE/PROPS for bound attributes, and so on. The runtime reads the flag instead of diffing blindly, so it only compares the parts of the vnode the flag says can change.

Now consider an element that has no dynamic text or props at all — only a ref, a v-bind to a vnode hook, or (as in the example above) a custom directive. Nothing about its rendered output ever changes, but Vue still needs to visit it on every patch, because a ref needs updating, a vnode hook needs calling, or a directive's updated/unmounted hook needs invoking at the right moment. That's exactly what the NEED_PATCH flag exists for: it tells the runtime "nothing here looks different, but visit it anyway — something non-visual depends on it."

The bug was that NEED_PATCH could get dropped specifically when that same element was also inside a v-for. The compiler's own v-for-specific optimizations and its patch-flag analysis for refs/hooks/directives didn't compose correctly, so an element that would have correctly carried NEED_PATCH on its own lost that flag once it was also a loop child. Without the flag, the runtime had no signal telling it to visit the element during a patch — so the directive's lifecycle hook for that specific element silently went uninvoked.

The Bug, the Issue, and the Fix

This wasn't a hunch — it's two tracked issues and a merged fix in Vue's own repository. Issue #12569, titled "Custom directive's unmounted event is not triggered on v-for element," reported exactly the symptom above. Issue #9239 reported the same underlying gap for ref callbacks on v-for children — the flag loss wasn't directive-specific, it affected every NEED_PATCH-only case: refs, vnode hooks, and custom directives alike.

The maintainer who fixed it, in PR #11682 ("preserve vnode lifecycle in stable v-for"), described the bug precisely: "When an element uses ref, vnodeHook, or custom directives, the patchFlag should be NEED_PATCH. However, when they are used together with v-for, the patchFlag gets lost." The fix tracks whether an element needs patching separately from whether it needs to stay a full "block" in the compiler's internal tree, and the v-for transform now adds NEED_PATCH back wherever one of these lifecycle-sensitive features is present. It shipped in Vue 3.5.41 (2026-08-05).

What that means for you in practice: if your package.json resolves vue to 3.5.41 or later — or anything on the current 3.5.43 — this is already fixed, and the example above behaves correctly: both mounted and unmounted fire for every row, every time. If you're pinned to an older 3.5.x release, or anywhere earlier in the Vue 3 line (one of the two issues this fix closed, #9239, was reported against 3.2.47), the gap is real and silent. The straightforward fix is upgrading to 3.5.41 or later; this article doesn't catalog a non-upgrade workaround, since the bug lives in the compiler's static analysis rather than in anything your component code controls — check the linked GitHub issues directly if you need to stay pinned for now.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

This is not the index-as-key bug. A separate, much more famous v-for mistake — using the array index as :key — causes Vue to reuse the wrong DOM node and misattribute state across reorders. That's a key-strategy problem you control by choosing a stable :key. The bug in this article happens even with a perfectly correct, stable :key — it's a compiler flag that was lost, not a key you chose wrong.

v-if and v-for on different elements of the same loop are unaffected. This specifically concerned "stable" v-for — a keyed loop with no structural directive (v-if/v-for) on the same element changing the number of children per iteration independent of the list itself. Combining v-for with v-if on the same tag is already discouraged by Vue's own style guide, and can throw a runtime reference error if the v-if expression depends on the v-for's loop variable — a separate, unrelated problem, not this bug.

Built-in reactive bindings were never affected. v-model, v-show, bound :class/:style/props, and interpolated text all carry their own patch flags (PROPS, STYLE, CLASS, TEXT) regardless of v-for. The gap was specific to elements whose only dynamic feature was a ref, a vnode hook, or a custom directive, with nothing else forcing a patch flag already.

ref callbacks silently missing inside v-for was the same bug. If you've ever seen a ref array (:ref="(el) => refs.push(el)") inside a loop skip an entry or hold a stale element after a list changed, issue #9239 describes the identical mechanism — not a separate problem to debug.

Custom directives using only created/beforeMount/beforeUpdate hooks were affected identically to mounted/unmounted. The bug was about the patch flag being present at all, not about which specific directive hook fires — every hook on the affected element went uninvoked on the patches where the flag was missing.

Best Practices

Reach for this knowledge when you maintain any directive that does real cleanup — removing listeners, destroying a third-party widget instance, disconnecting a ResizeObserver or MutationObserver — and that directive is ever used inside a list. Confirm your installed Vue is 3.5.41 or later before trusting that cleanup unconditionally.

Avoid relying on directive lifecycle hooks for anything correctness-critical even after upgrading. Directives are the right tool for DOM-only side effects (focus management, third-party widget wiring, scroll/intersection observers) — not for application state that must be perfectly consistent, where a watch or computed-driven reactive update gives you a mechanism entirely outside the compiler's patch-flag analysis.

Write a real regression test for list-cleanup directives, not just a manual click-through: mount a list with the directive, remove an item, and assert the directive's unmounted hook actually ran for it. This bug shipped silently for years precisely because it only reproduces once an item leaves a loop — a test that only ever mounts, never removes, would never have caught it.

Pin and read your Vue version deliberately, especially on a long-lived app. npm ls vue (or checking the lockfile) tells you exactly what you're running; npm view vue dist-tags tells you what's current. A multi-year-old pin anywhere before 3.5.41 is exactly the situation this bug could still be lurking in.

FAQ

Why didn't Vue throw an error or a dev-mode warning for this?

Because nothing about the element's own rendering was wrong — the DOM node itself unmounted correctly along with its parent list item. The only thing missing was Vue's internal signal to also invoke the directive's hook on that specific vnode. There was no incorrect state for Vue to detect and warn about; the gap was an omission in the compiler's static analysis, not a runtime contradiction it could catch.

Does this affect v-model or other built-in directives?

No. v-model compiles to a bound prop plus an event listener, both of which already carry their own patch flags (PROPS) independent of this bug. The gap only touched elements whose sole dynamic feature was a ref, a vnode hook, or a custom directive with nothing else forcing a patch flag.

Is Nuxt affected the same way?

Yes, to the extent any given Nuxt app's resolved vue dependency was on an affected version — Nuxt renders on top of Vue's own core, so this is a Vue-core fix, not something Nuxt layers on. Check vue's resolved version in your Nuxt project's lockfile the same way you would in a plain Vue app.

Is this fixed in Vue 2?

Not applicable — Vue 2's compiler doesn't use this patch-flag/block system at all (it was introduced with Vue 3's rewritten renderer), so the bug and its fix are both Vue-3-specific.

How do I confirm my own app isn't exposed?

Check your resolved vue version (npm ls vue), and if it's below 3.5.41, reproduce the repro in this article in a scratch component before deciding whether to upgrade immediately or schedule it — a directive that only logs, with no real side effect, costs nothing to leave broken; one that owns a listener or a third-party instance is worth fixing promptly.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 9-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

Cheat Sheet

Task What to check Notes
Confirm you're affected npm ls vue Affected: any Vue 3 release before 3.5.41 (reported as far back as 3.2.47)
Confirm you're fixed Vue ≥ 3.5.41 (current: 3.5.43) No flag, no config — the fix is purely internal
Reproduce the symptom Custom directive + keyed v-for + remove an item Log mounted/unmounted; on affected versions only mounted appears
Tell it apart from index-as-key bugs Does it happen with a correct, stable :key? This bug happens even with a correct key; index-as-key is a separate mistake
Root cause, one line NEED_PATCH patch flag dropped for ref/vnode-hook/directive-only elements inside v-for vuejs/core#11682
What's NOT affected v-model, bound :class/:style/props, interpolated text These already carry their own patch flags regardless of v-for 
// A directive you can trust inside v-for, once Vue is ≥ 3.5.41:
const vCleanupCheck = {
  mounted(el, binding) {
    el.__cleanup = () => console.log(`cleaned up row ${binding.value}`)
  },
  unmounted(el, binding) {
    el.__cleanup?.()
  },
}
// Regression-test it: mount a list, remove an item, assert unmounted ran.

Key Takeaways

  • A custom directive's mounted/unmounted hooks could silently fail to fire for an element inside a keyed v-for, with no error or warning — fixed in Vue 3.5.41.
  • The cause was a compiler detail: elements whose only dynamic feature is a ref, a vnode hook, or a custom directive need the NEED_PATCH flag to be visited during a patch, and that flag could get lost specifically when combined with v-for.
  • This is unrelated to the index-as-key mistake — it happened even with a correct, stable :key.
  • If you maintain a directive that does real cleanup, confirm your Vue version is 3.5.41 or later, and write a test that actually removes a list item rather than only mounting one.

The listener nobody was tracking is the quiet failure mode that makes this bug worth knowing even now that it's fixed: it never crashed, never logged a warning, and would have kept accumulating in a long-running single-page app for as long as the affected Vue version stayed pinned. Compiler-level bugs like this are rare, but they're exactly why "it works when I click it once" isn't the same as "it works" — the loop is where cleanup earns its keep.

Have you run into a directive that seemed to stop working only inside a list, or found another case where NEED_PATCH mattered? Drop it in the comments.
