articles.title: Your console.log() Might Be Slowing Down Your App
articles.description: Most of us use console.log() every day.  Checking an API response? console.log().  Debugging a loop?...
articles.body_html:
Most of us use console.log() every day.

Checking an API response? console.log().

Debugging a loop? console.log().

Trying to figure out why something isn't working? Another console.log().

It's one of the simplest debugging tools in JavaScript. But there's something we often overlook: logging isn't free, and too much of it can affect performance.

Let's understand why and how to avoid it.

First, what is the Console API?

The Console API gives us methods to print messages, inspect values, and debug our applications.

Some commonly used methods are:

Method Purpose
console.log() Print general messages
console.info() Display information
console.warn() Show warnings
console.error() Report errors
console.table() Display data in a table
console.time() Measure execution time

Here's a simple example:

const user = { name: "John", age: 25 };

console.log(user);
console.table([user]);
console.warn("Something needs attention!");

Nothing complicated, right?

But here's an interesting detail.

console isn't actually part of the JavaScript language itself.

Who provides console? JavaScript or the browser?

JavaScript follows a specification called ECMAScript.

That specification defines things like variables, functions, objects, arrays, and promises.

But it doesn't define console.

Instead, console is provided by the environment where JavaScript runs.

  • Browsers provide it through their developer tools.
  • Node.js provides its own console implementation.
  • Other runtimes can implement it differently.

That's why console behavior and performance can vary between environments.

The problem: Logging inside loops

Imagine you're processing 10,000 records.

While debugging, you add a simple log:

const records = Array.from(
  { length: 10_000 },
  (_, index) => index
);

for (const record of records) {
  console.log(record);
}

Looks harmless.

But this loop doesn't just process 10,000 records. It also asks the runtime to handle 10,000 logging operations.

Depending on the environment, those operations may involve formatting values, passing messages to developer tools, or writing output.

And all that work takes time.

How much slower can it get?

In one local test, the results looked like this:

Test Measured time
Single console.log() call 0.003 ms
1,000 calls inside a loop 26.4 ms

These are example measurements, not universal benchmarks. Actual results depend on the browser, runtime, machine, output size, and whether DevTools is open.

The important point is simple:

A tiny cost repeated thousands of times can become noticeable.

And even if your browser groups repeated messages into one line, it doesn't mean the logging calls were skipped.

How can we avoid this?

The good news is that we don't need to stop using console.log().

We just need to use it carefully.

1. Remove unnecessary logs

Debug logs are useful while developing, but most don't need to stay in production.

Instead of:

for (const user of users) {
  console.log("Processing:", user);
  processUser(user);
}

Keep it simple:

for (const user of users) {
  processUser(user);
}

If you need to know how many users were processed, log a summary instead of every individual record.

for (const user of users) {
  processUser(user);
}

console.info(`Processed ${users.length} users`);

One useful message is often better than thousands of repeated messages.

2. Create a simple logger

If you frequently debug your application, a small logger can help.

const isDevelopment =
  process.env.NODE_ENV !== "production";

export const logger = {
  log: (...args) => {
    if (isDevelopment) {
      console.log(...args);
    }
  },

  warn: (...args) => {
    if (isDevelopment) {
      console.warn(...args);
    }
  },

  error: (...args) => {
    console.error(...args);
  },
};

Now use it anywhere:

logger.log("User loaded successfully");
logger.warn("Response is taking longer");
logger.error("Failed to load user");

In production, debug messages won't be printed.

Just remember that calling a no-op logger still has a small cost, especially if you're calculating expensive values before passing them to it. Also, process.env.NODE_ENV must be supported or replaced by your build tool.

3. Remove console calls during the build

If your project uses Terser, you can configure it to remove console statements when building for production.

For example:

// vite.config.js
import { defineConfig } from "vite";

export default defineConfig({
  build: {
    minify: "terser",
    terserOptions: {
      compress: {
        drop_console: ["log", "debug", "info"],
      },
    },
  },
});

This removes the selected console methods from the production bundle.

Notice that we haven't removed console.error().

That's intentional.

One important thing: Don't blindly remove every console call. Some messages are useful for troubleshooting real production issues. Build-time removal can also remove argument expressions, so avoid relying on side effects inside logging calls.

4. Keep important error reporting

Not every console message is unnecessary.

For example:

try {
  await saveUser(user);
} catch (error) {
  console.error("Failed to save user:", error);
}

Errors are worth recording.

For larger production applications, a proper logging or error-monitoring system is even better. It helps you understand failures without depending entirely on browser console output.

Just make sure you don't accidentally log passwords, tokens, or sensitive user information.

A small habit that makes a difference

console.log() isn't bad.

It's incredibly useful, and there's no reason to avoid it while debugging.

The problem starts when we leave unnecessary logs in frequently executed code, especially loops, rendering logic, and high-traffic paths.

A few things worth remembering:

  • Avoid logging every iteration of a large loop.
  • Remove unnecessary debug messages before production.
  • Use a simple logger when it makes sense.
  • Configure your build tools to strip unwanted logs.
  • Keep meaningful error reporting.

You probably won't notice a performance difference from removing two or three logs.

But removing thousands of unnecessary logging operations from a hot path? That can make a real difference.

The takeaway: Use the console to understand your code, not to slow it down.

Have you ever found unnecessary console.log() calls causing performance issues in a project?

I'd love to hear about it! 👇

articles.title: Python 3.14's concurrent.interpreters module turns a 3.6-second GIL bottleneck into 0.9 seconds
articles.description: I measured Python 3.14's new subinterpreters against threads and processes: 3.6s of GIL contention dropped to 0.9s, but a single interpreter flatly refuses a second concurrent thread.
articles.body_html:
A CPU-bound Python job split across four threads took 3.6 seconds on my machine. The same job split across four of Python 3.14's new subinterpreters took 0.9 seconds, roughly what one thread alone takes to do a quarter of the work. That part matched what I expected from the PEP. What I did not expect was that asking one of those subinterpreters to run two things at once does not slow it down. It refuses outright.

concurrent.interpreters is new in the standard library as of Python 3.14, released on 7 October 2026. Subinterpreters themselves are not new - they have existed in the C API since Python 1.5 and CPython has used them internally for years - but PEP 734 is what makes them usable from ordinary Python code, with no C extension required. Each subinterpreter gets its own Global Interpreter Lock, which is the part worth testing: it is the thing that is supposed to let CPU-bound Python code actually use more than one core without reaching for multiprocessing.

I tested it against a CPU-bound workload (counting primes below 400,000, a plain Python double loop with no C extensions to hide behind), compared against threads, processes, and a single thread, three runs each, inside a python:3.14-slim container with four cores available.

The headline number

approach time for 4x the work
single thread (1x unit, for reference) 0.77 - 0.80s
4 OS threads, classic GIL 3.51 - 3.70s
4 subinterpreters (new in 3.14) 0.89 - 0.98s
4 processes (multiprocessing) 0.95 - 1.30s

Four threads doing four units of CPU-bound work took more than four times as long as one thread doing one unit - 3.6s against roughly 0.8s, which is actually a bit worse than the 3.2s you'd get from perfect serialisation, because the GIL has to keep stopping one thread to let another run. Four subinterpreters doing the same four units took about 0.9s: close enough to the single-unit baseline that the extra three units of work were, for practical purposes, free. That is real parallelism, not a scheduling trick, and it lands in the same place multiprocessing already does.

What it refuses: one thread per interpreter, not shared

The PEP's selling point is that each interpreter has its own GIL. I wanted to see what happens when two threads try to use one interpreter's GIL at the same time, expecting it to behave like classic Python: both threads run, the shared GIL makes them take turns.

That is not what happened. A single Interpreter object only tolerates one caller. A second concurrent call doesn't queue, and it doesn't share time with the first - it is rejected immediately:

Exception in thread Thread-2 (_call):
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.14/concurrent/interpreters/__init__.py", line 226, in _call
    res, excinfo = _interpreters.call(self._id, callable, args, kwargs, restrict=True)
concurrent.interpreters.InterpreterError: interpreter already running

I confirmed the shape of this with three variants of the same interpreter, run in sequence:

scenario time outcome
one call 0.84s fine
two sequential calls, same interpreter 1.63s fine, roughly 2x
two concurrent calls, same interpreter 0.84s wall-clock second call raises InterpreterError

interpreters.create() is documented as returning "a new (idle) Python interpreter", and that word is accurate: idle or running, nothing in between. If you want N things running at once, you need N interpreters, one each. A thread pool aimed at a single shared interpreter - the pattern every ThreadPoolExecutor tutorial uses with regular threads - does not translate. You get one interpreter's worth of work and an exception, not graceful serialisation.

The opposite number: interpreters are not obviously cheaper to start than processes

The other assumption I walked in with was that subinterpreters, being lighter than OS processes, would be cheap to spin up. I measured the cost of creating four workers and giving each one some real state (a 200,000-element list), steady state after the first warm-up run:

approach create + populate, 4 workers
fork (Python 3.13's Linux default) 0.037 - 0.038s
forkserver (Python 3.14's Linux default) 0.057 - 0.065s
4 subinterpreters 0.076 - 0.078s

Creating four subinterpreters and running a small amount of code in each took about twice as long as a classic fork-based process pool, and somewhat longer than the new forkserver default too. None of this matters once the work inside each worker takes more than a few milliseconds - the 3.6s-versus-0.9s number above swallows an 80-millisecond setup cost without noticing. But it means "subinterpreters are lighter than processes" is not something I could verify at creation time; the saving, where it exists, is in not forking a second copy of the process's address space, not in any faster start.

That forkserver row was an accident. I wrote a timing script that called multiprocessing.Process(...).start() directly from the module's top level, the way plenty of tutorial code still does, and it crashed:

RuntimeError:
        An attempt has been made to start a new process before the
        current process has finished its bootstrapping phase.

Checking multiprocessing.get_start_method() explained it: Python 3.14 changed the default start method on Linux from fork to forkserver. Python 3.13 reports fork; 3.14 reports forkserver. forkserver re-imports your module in the child, which is exactly the thing if __name__ == "__main__": exists to guard against, and which fork never required you to bother with. Every piece of multiprocessing code I'd written without that guard over the years happened to work by accident, on Linux, until this release. It's a one-line fix, but it is a real break, and it landed in the same release that gives you an alternative that doesn't have this problem at all.

What it costs: closing an interpreter doesn't give the memory back

I ran four rounds of "create four interpreters, give each a 200,000-element list, close them", watching my own process's RSS the whole time:

round 1: 16920 -> 55648 KB
round 2: 55648 -> 57140 KB
round 3: 57140 -> 59476 KB
round 4: 59476 -> 61096 KB

.close() does finalise the interpreter - a destroyed interpreter can't be called again, and I checked that it raises if you try - but the process's resident memory never drops back to where it started. It flattens out (each later round adds less than the first) rather than growing without bound, which looks like CPython's allocator holding onto freed arenas rather than a genuine leak, but I didn't chase that further. If you're planning to cycle through many short-lived interpreters inside one long-running process, budget for that memory to stay resident, not to be returned to the OS the way a finished process's memory is.

What's actually shareable between interpreters

Subinterpreters don't share objects by default - that is the entire point, it's what lets them skip the GIL - so most interesting values need to cross a boundary. is_shareable() gives a yes/no answer per type:

int              -> True
str              -> True
bytes            -> True
None             -> True
bool             -> True
tuple of ints    -> True
float            -> True
list             -> False
dict             -> False

Passing a threading.Lock as an argument to Interpreter.call() fails immediately, with the repr of the offending object right there in the message:

NotShareableError: (<unlocked _thread.lock object at 0x7f61b8b5add0>,) does not support cross-interpreter data

An ordinary custom class instance fails the same way, with a flatter message:

NotShareableError: object does not support cross-interpreter data

But the cross-interpreter Queue that the same module provides does not enforce this. I put a plain custom-class instance onto a queue and it went through without complaint, and came back out as a distinct, working object with the same attribute values - the queue silently pickles and unpickles it:

q = interpreters.create_queue()
q.put(Thing())          # no error
received = q.get()
# received is not the original object, but received.value is unchanged

So "not shareable" is enforced differently depending on how the object crosses over. A direct argument to call() is checked against the strict shareable-types list and rejected on the spot. The same object dropped into a Queue gets the softer treatment the docs describe for put(): pickled going in, unpickled coming out as a new, unrelated object. If your code passes data between interpreters by argument, moving it to a queue instead buys you a much larger set of types - at the cost of identity and, for anything mutable, of staying in sync with the original.

What I got wrong on the way

My first attempt at the shareability tests put several checks in one script with no if __name__ == "__main__": guard, calling interp.call() with a mix of shareable and non-shareable arguments one after another. Running it printed every result twice, and the second copy sometimes disagreed with the first about which error got raised. My best explanation, which I didn't fully verify, is that call()'s documented pickle fallback needs to resolve names against the target interpreter's own __main__, and since that interpreter had never run my module, resolving anything defined at module level meant running the whole module there first - silently re-executing my test file a second time, inside the subinterpreter, with its own fresh state. Splitting each check into its own small script with a proper __main__ guard made every result reproducible, which is what's reported above. I'd treat any subinterpreter test that imports a lot of top-level code as suspect until it survives being run twice.

Run it yourself

This needs Python 3.14 and four-ish cores to see the gap clearly. I ran it in Docker because that's the fastest way to get an exact version:

docker pull python:3.14-slim

The core benchmark:

# bench.py
import time, threading, sys

def cpu_work(n):
    count = 0
    for i in range(2, n):
        is_prime = True
        for d in range(2, int(i ** 0.5) + 1):
            if i % d == 0:
                is_prime = False
                break
        if is_prime:
            count += 1
    return count

def run_threads(n, workers):
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=cpu_work, args=(n,)) for _ in range(workers)]
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for t in threads: t.start()
    for t in threads: t.join()
    print(f"threads={workers}: {time.perf_counter()-t0:.3f}s")

def run_interpreters(n, workers):
    import concurrent.interpreters as interpreters
    interps = [interpreters.create() for _ in range(workers)]
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    threads = [i.call_in_thread(cpu_work, n) for i in interps]
    for t in threads: t.join()
    print(f"interpreters={workers}: {time.perf_counter()-t0:.3f}s")
    for i in interps: i.close()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mode, n, workers = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2]), int(sys.argv[3])
    {"threads": run_threads, "interpreters": run_interpreters}[mode](n, workers)

docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/w -w /w python:3.14-slim python3 bench.py threads 400000 4
docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/w -w /w python:3.14-slim python3 bench.py interpreters 400000 4

And the refusal, which needs no setup at all:

docker run --rm python:3.14-slim python3 -c "
import concurrent.interpreters as interpreters
i = interpreters.create()
t1 = i.call_in_thread(lambda: __import__('time').sleep(1))
t2 = i.call_in_thread(lambda: __import__('time').sleep(1))
t1.join(); t2.join()
"

What to do with this

If you have a CPU-bound Python workload that multiprocessing already parallelises well, subinterpreters aren't an obvious upgrade yet: on this release they start up slower than a plain fork and about the same as forkserver, and you still need one interpreter per concurrent task, with no pooling against a single interpreter. Where they're worth trying now is the code that currently reaches for a thread, because threading is simpler to wire up than multiprocessing, and then quietly gets nothing from the GIL: swap the Thread for an Interpreter.call_in_thread, and check your data either fits the shareable-types list or is willing to cross as a pickled copy through a Queue. And if you have multiprocessing code anywhere that starts a Process without an if __name__ == "__main__": guard, fix that first - 3.14 will find it on Linux even if nothing else in this post applies to you.

articles.title: Your secrets don't need a git commit to leak into an AI tool

articles.body_html:
Most of us have the "don't commit secrets" reflex drilled in. Pre-commit hooks, secret scanners in CI, .env in .gitignore. Good. That covers the repo.

It doesn't cover the context window.

The gap: the repo is not the boundary anymore

When you work with an AI coding assistant, what leaves your machine isn't just the file you're editing. It's whatever you paste, whatever the extension decides is relevant, and whatever the agent reads while it's "helping." The security boundary now includes the editor extension, the chat history, any telemetry, and every service that processes that context on the way to the model and back.

Secret scanners watch commits. Nothing in a typical setup watches what you paste into a chat panel at 6pm while a deploy is failing.

Here are the usual ways a secret ends up in context without ever touching git.

1. The failing test that prints its config

An integration test fails. The assertion message helpfully dumps the client object, which includes the connection string with the password inline. You copy the whole test output into the assistant and ask "why is this failing?"

The question was about the assertion. The payload included the credential.

2. The environment dump 

$ env | sort
...
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...
DATABASE_URL=postgres://app:...@db.internal:5432/prod
STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=sk_live_...

"Here's my environment, why can't the app find the config?" is a completely normal debugging move. It's also the fastest way to hand over every key on the box in one paste. Agents that can run shell commands can do this on their own if you let them.

3. Logs that log too much

A verbose HTTP client logs request headers. One of them is Authorization: Bearer .... You paste 200 lines of log to get help with a timeout, and line 143 is a live token.

4. The copied snippet

Someone shares a "working example" in Slack with the key still in it. You paste it into the assistant to adapt it. Now it's in two systems you don't control instead of one.

(These are illustrative scenarios, not specific incidents, but if you've debugged anything under pressure you've probably seen at least one.)

What actually helps

  • Minimize what you send. Paste the relevant ten lines, not the whole log. Ask about the error, not the environment.
  • Redact before pasting. Mask tokens, connection strings and headers. A small shell function or editor snippet that scrubs obvious patterns is worth having.
  • Scope your credentials. If a dev key does leak, it should only be able to touch dev. Short-lived, least-privilege keys shrink the blast radius.
  • Check how your tool handles data. What's retained, for how long, whether it's used for training, what the extension sends automatically, where telemetry goes. These are often separate settings and separate policies. One "privacy" toggle rarely answers all of them.
  • Restrict what agents can read. If your assistant can open files and run commands, keep .env, credential files and secret stores out of its reach.

If it already happened

Deleting the chat message is not remediation. You don't know what was logged, cached or forwarded before you hit delete. Treat it like any other exposure: rotate the credential, revoke the old one, check access logs for use.

The reframe

Secret management used to be a version control problem. With AI tools in the loop, it's a data-flow problem: anything that reaches the model's context has, to some degree, left your control.

The safest secret is the one that never enters the context in the first place.

How does your team handle this today? Do you have any tooling that checks what goes into an AI assistant, or is it all down to developer habit?

articles.body_html:
1. Introduction

When developing an application or service, one of the common questions we face is how many concurrent requests it can handle and how the services it depends on will respond. Even if we verify that all functionalities work correctly, this does not guarantee that the system will maintain its performance as demand increases.

This is why software testing goes beyond verifying functional requirements. It also allows us to evaluate aspects such as performance, stability, and responsiveness. In particular, load testing is not simply about pushing a system until it fails, but rather about understanding how it behaves under different conditions and identifying when it stops meeting the expected requirements.

In the previous article, we built a service to identify duplicate products using Amazon Bedrock, S3 Vectors, and DynamoDB, including an AWS Lambda function to perform real-time searches. During our initial tests, the service responded within a few seconds, but one question remained unanswered: how would it behave if many users accessed it simultaneously?

To answer this question, in this second part, we will expose the service through Amazon API Gateway and evaluate its behavior under load. Before running the tests, however, we need to define what we want to measure and which criteria we will use to evaluate the results. To do this, we will introduce some fundamental concepts of Site Reliability Engineering (SRE). We will then automate load testing with Grafana k6 on AWS and, finally, generate a report in which generative AI will help us interpret the collected metrics.

2. Understanding Site Reliability Engineering (SRE)

2.1. What Is SRE?

Before evaluating how our API behaves under load, we need to establish what acceptable performance and reliability actually mean. A service may continue responding to requests, but that does not necessarily mean it is meeting the expected performance requirements.

This is where Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) comes into play. Originally developed at Google, SRE is a discipline that applies software engineering principles to operating and maintaining reliable systems. It focuses on defining measurable objectives, selecting indicators that reflect service behavior, and using automation to reduce repetitive operational tasks.
For our use case, these concepts provide a foundation for moving beyond simply checking whether the API responds. Instead, we can evaluate specific indicators such as response times, error rates, and performance under different load conditions.

2.2. Seven Principles of SRE

SRE is built on a set of principles that guide how reliable services are designed, operated, and maintained. These range from defining reliability objectives and managing risk to automation, monitoring, and keeping systems as simple as possible.
The following infographic summarizes seven of these principles, based on Google's Site Reliability Engineering book.


Illustration by the author. Based on Google's Site Reliability Engineering book.

2.3. Capacity Planning and Performance

Service reliability depends not only on availability but also on the ability to handle demand while maintaining acceptable performance. In this context, SRE includes several practices aimed at anticipating problems, optimizing resources, and reducing the impact of changes in production.

Among these practices, we can highlight:

  • Capacity Planning: ensuring that a system has sufficient resources and redundancy to handle expected demand without compromising availability objectives. To support this, Google recommends regular load testing to assess the actual capacity of a service.
  • Efficiency and Performance: understanding how performance changes as load increases, identifying potential degradation, and finding opportunities to optimize resource utilization.
  • Change Management: reducing the risks associated with changes in production. According to Google's documented experience, approximately 70% of service outages are caused by changes to live systems, highlighting the importance of detecting problems early. These practices are directly related to our use case, as we aim to evaluate our API's performance under different load conditions.

2.4. SLI, SLO, and SLA

Evaluating a service's capacity and performance requires more than simply running tests and collecting metrics. We also need to define what we want to measure and which service levels we consider acceptable.

In this context, SRE introduces three related concepts: SLI (Service Level Indicator), SLO (Service Level Objective), and SLA (Service Level Agreement). Together, they connect technical measurements with service objectives and commitments.

The following infographic summarizes what each concept represents, the question it helps answer, and a practical example of how it can be applied.


Illustration by the author. Based on Google's SRE framework.

3. Grafana k6: A Tool for Performance Testing

Grafana k6 is an open-source tool developed in Go and maintained by Grafana Labs, designed to perform load and performance testing on applications, APIs, and microservices. Test scenarios are defined using JavaScript, making it easier to automate tests and integrate them into development workflows.

Although we often associate these tools with stress testing, k6 allows us to evaluate how a system behaves under different load conditions, without necessarily pushing it to the point of failure.


Illustration by the author. Based on Grafana k6 documentation.

3.1. Types of Load Tests

Depending on what we want to evaluate, we can define different test scenarios:

  • Smoke: verify that the system responds correctly under minimal load.
  • Average-load: evaluate system behavior under normal operating conditions.
  • Stress: assess how the system responds under high load.
  • Soak: identify potential performance degradation when load is sustained over extended periods.
  • Spike: evaluate how the system responds to sudden increases in traffic.
  • Breakpoint: progressively increase the load to identify the point at which the system stops meeting the expected criteria. These scenarios allow us to analyze different aspects of system performance. We should also consider that an application often depends on multiple components and services, meaning that performance degradation can originate from different parts of its architecture.

3.2. Main Components of k6

To execute these tests, k6 provides several components that allow us to configure load, validate responses, collect metrics, and integrate results with other tools.


Illustration by the author. Based on Grafana k6 documentation.

We can group them into four main components:

  • ⚙️ Options: define how a test will be executed. They allow us to configure scenarios, load stages, virtual users (VUs), duration, iterations, and acceptance thresholds. These options enable us to reproduce the different types of tests described earlier.
  • ✅ Checks: validate conditions on received responses, such as HTTP status codes or response content. A failed check is recorded in the metrics but does not automatically stop the test execution.
  • 📊 Metrics: collect information about system behavior, including response times, request counts, and error rates. k6 provides built-in metrics and supports custom metrics.
  • 🔗 Integrations: allow tests to be incorporated into CI/CD pipelines and results to be exported to storage, monitoring, and visualization tools. In our case, we will use CSV and JSON to store the results and subsequently process the metrics included in the final report.

4. Architecture

Our load testing solution builds on the game-catalog-resolve-product Lambda function developed in the previous article, which uses Amazon Bedrock, S3 Vectors, and DynamoDB to identify duplicate products.

In this second part, we expose the function through Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) with IAM authorization, requiring k6 requests to be signed using AWS credentials.

The testing process is automated using AWS Step Functions, which orchestrates k6 execution on Amazon ECS Fargate and subsequent report generation through an AWS Lambda function. Test scripts and results are stored in Amazon S3, while Amazon ECR stores the container images.

The entire infrastructure is defined using Terraform, and the code is available on GitHub, making the solution reproducible.


Architecture diagram by the author.

5. Use Case: Automated Load Testing

In this use case, we will run different load testing scenarios against our API. To do this, we use Grafana k6 running inside a Docker container to send requests and collect performance metrics. Once the tests are complete, a Python-based process calculates the results and generates a PDF report that includes an interpretation provided by Amazon Bedrock.


Illustration by the author.

5.1. The Repository

The project is available on GitHub: game-catalog-k6.

RominaElenaMendezEscobar / game-catalog-k6

Load testing a GenAI API on AWS with k6: scenarios defined in JSON (smoke, load, stress, spike) run on ECS Fargate and orchestrated by Step Functions. Metrics from k6 and CloudWatch are collected by Lambda, and Amazon Bedrock generates an analysis of the results. Tests an API Gateway endpoint backed by Lambda, Amazon Bedrock and S3 Vectors.

⚡ Automated API Load Testing on AWS: Grafana k6 and AI-Powered Reporting with Amazon Bedrock

Serverless pipeline that runs Grafana k6 load tests against an API on Amazon ECS Fargate orchestrated by AWS Step Functions, and generates a PDF report where Amazon Bedrock interprets the metrics. All the infrastructure is defined with Terraform.

📝 Article: 🔗 Part 1 (the API under test): Identical or Similar? AI-Powered Product Matching with Amazon Bedrock and S3 Vectors · repository

🎯 What it does

  1. Runs a load test with k6 in a container on ECS Fargate, using a configurable scenario (smoke, load, stress, spike).
  2. Stores every run in its own S3 folder, with the results and an exact copy of the scenario used.
  3. Generates a PDF report: metrics are computed by code; Amazon Bedrock only interprets them, and the figures it quotes are validated against the computed metrics.

The thresholds…

View on GitHub

Its structure includes the k6 scripts, test scenarios, report generator, and infrastructure defined using Terraform.
game-catalog-k6/
├── Dockerfile, entrypoint.sh
├── search.js, sigv4.js
├── scenarios/
├── queries.json
├── report/
│   └── config/
├── terraform/
└── build-and-push.sh

The goal is to make this solution reusable for testing other APIs without modifying the underlying infrastructure or the report generation process. To do this, we only need to configure three elements:

  • 〰️ The API we want to test
  • 〰️ The requests we want to send
  • 〰️ The load testing scenarios

5.2. Configuring Tests for Another API

1. Identify the API: api_id

In our case, we use Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) with IAM authorization. The service URL follows this structure:

https://<api-id>.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com

The API identifier can be found in the AWS Management Console under API Gateway → Your API → API details.
To configure the project, we specify it in terraform/terraform.tfvars:

api_id = "<api-id>"

Terraform uses this identifier to construct the API URL and configure the necessary permissions for the k6 container to invoke the API using IAM-signed requests.

2. Define the Requests: queries.json

Once we have identified the API, we need to define which requests we want to send.
Our API accepts text searches through POST /search. To define the requests executed during testing, we use the queries.json file, which contains different video game searches in English and Spanish.

[
  {"query": "fifa 14 ps3 digital code", "lang": "en"},
  {"query": "fifa 14 ps3 codigo digital", "lang": "es"},
  {"query": "gta vice city ps2", "lang": "en"},
  {"query": "el mario kart de la wii", "lang": "es"}
]

If the API expects a different request structure, we will also need to adapt the request body in search.js.

3. Configure the Load: scenarios

Once we have defined what to request, we need to establish how the load will be applied. For this, we use JSON files in the scenarios/ directory, each with its own configuration.

Each JSON file defines a different load testing scenario:

  • smoke.json — Smoke Test: 1 virtual user for 1 minute to verify basic functionality.
  • load.json — Load Test: 5 virtual users for 5 minutes to evaluate system behavior under steady load.
  • stress.json — Stress Test: gradually increases the load from 5 to 40 virtual users over 6 minutes to identify performance degradation.
  • spike.json — Spike Test: increases the load from 0 to 50 virtual users in 30 seconds to evaluate how the system responds to sudden traffic spikes. Each scenario can be customized by adjusting the number of virtual users, test duration, load pattern, and performance thresholds.

Each file allows us to configure virtual users, test duration, load patterns, and performance thresholds.
For example, smoke.json contains:

{
  "name": "smoke",
  "description": "1 user for 1 minute: checks that the API works before adding load.",
  "queries_file": "queries.json",
  "endpoint": "/search",
  "think_time_seconds": 1,
  "executor": {
    "executor": "constant-vus",
    "vus": 1,
    "duration": "1m"
  },
  "thresholds": {
    "http_req_failed": ["rate<0.01"],
    "http_req_duration": ["p(95)<5000"]
  }
}

The main parameters are:

  • endpoint: the API path to which requests will be sent.
  • think_time_seconds: the pause between requests made by each virtual user.
  • executor: defines the load pattern, number of virtual users, and test duration.
  • thresholds: allows us to define acceptance criteria for the metrics. In this example, an error rate below 1% and a p95 response time below 5 seconds. These thresholds allow us to translate our performance objectives into measurable acceptance criteria during testing, following the SLI and SLO concepts introduced earlier. We can modify existing scenarios or create new JSON files to evaluate different load conditions while reusing the same k6 code.

5.3. Deploying the Infrastructure with Terraform

Once the configuration files are ready, we can deploy the solution using AWS CloudShell, with the tools needed to run Terraform and build Docker images.

1. Install Terraform (First Time Only)

AWS CloudShell does not include Terraform by default. We can download it to our home directory, which persists across sessions:

curl -sLo /tmp/terraform.zip https://releases.hashicorp.com/terraform/1.9.8/terraform_1.9.8_linux_amd64.zip
mkdir -p ~/bin && unzip -o /tmp/terraform.zip -d ~/bin
echo 'export PATH="HOME/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.bashrc && source ~/.bashrc
terraform version

2. Create the Infrastructure 

git clone https://github.com/RominaElenaMendezEscobar/game-catalog-k6.git
cd game-catalog-k6/terraform
echo 'api_id = "<api-id>"' > terraform.tfvars
terraform init
terraform apply \
  -target=aws_ecr_repository.k6 \
  -target=aws_ecr_repository.report
../build-and-push.sh

terraform apply

The deployment is performed in three stages: first, we create the Amazon ECR repositories; next, we build and push the container images; and finally, we deploy the remaining resources.

Terraform provisions the required infrastructure, including Amazon ECS Fargate, AWS Step Functions, AWS Lambda, Amazon S3, and IAM roles and permissions. It also uploads the test scenarios and queries that k6 will use to Amazon S3.

5.4. Running a Load Test

With the infrastructure deployed, we can start a test execution using AWS Step Functions, specifying the scenario we want to run.
For example, to execute load.json:

aws stepfunctions start-execution \
  --state-machine-arn "$(terraform output -raw state_machine_arn)" \
  --input '{"scenario": "load", "label": "baseline"}'


Screenshot by the author. AWS Management Console.

The state machine orchestrates three steps:

  • PrepareRun: takes the scenario and label provided in the input and generates a unique identifier based on the date and time (run_id). This identifier is used in the following two steps to ensure that the results and report are associated with the same test execution.
  • RunLoadTest: starts the k6 container on Amazon ECS Fargate, executes the selected scenario, and stores the results in Amazon S3.
  • GenerateReport: processes the results using an AWS Lambda function, calculates the metrics, and generates a PDF report with an interpretation provided by Amazon Bedrock. Each execution is stored in a separate folder, following a structure such as runs/<scenario>/<date>/, along with the configuration used for the test.


Screenshot by the author. Amazon S3 bucket showing the files and results generated by the automated load testing pipeline.

Generated by k6 (RunLoadTest):

  • k6-summary.json: a summary of the test, including aggregated metric values (averages, percentiles, error rates) and threshold evaluation results.
  • k6-results.csv: detailed data for each request, including when it was sent, how long it took, and whether it failed. This data is used to generate time-series charts.
  • run-info.json: execution metadata, including the scenario, label, timestamps, k6 version, and container image.
  • scripts/: an exact copy of the scripts and scenarios used, allowing us to reproduce the test configuration even if the original files are modified later. #### Generated by the Report Lambda (GenerateReport):
  • metrics.json: metrics calculated by the code using the files generated during the test.
  • ai-analysis.json: the interpretation generated by Amazon Bedrock, along with the results of the numerical validation.
  • report.pdf: the final report, combining all the information above. To run a different test scenario, we only need to change the scenario value in the Step Functions execution input.

5.5. Report Generation

Once the test is complete, the pipeline processes the k6 results and generates a PDF report that combines the calculated metrics with an interpretation provided by Amazon Bedrock.
For this stage, we use an AWS Lambda function deployed as a container image, as we need several Python libraries: pandas for data processing, matplotlib for generating charts, and fpdf2 for creating the PDF document.

Unlike traditional ZIP-based deployments, which have a 250 MB uncompressed size limit, AWS Lambda supports container images of up to 10 GB. This makes it easier to package the code and its dependencies into a reproducible environment while maintaining a serverless execution model.

The following infographic summarizes the main benefits of this approach.


Illustration by the author. Based on AWS Lambda documentation.

The container image is built using a Dockerfile and pushed to Amazon ECR. Terraform then configures the AWS Lambda function to use this image, as illustrated in the following workflow.


Illustration by the author. Based on AWS documentation.

We can view an example of the generated PDF report at the following link:
github.com report.pdf


Report generated by the author using Python, Grafana k6, and Amazon Bedrock.

The report consists of several pages organized into the following sections:

  • Test Context: the executed scenario (load, duration, and thresholds) and the test environment (k6 version, container image, and location of the results).
  • Results and Metrics: requests, throughput, error rates, p50, p95, and p99 latencies, threshold compliance, and a breakdown of each phase of a request.
  • Performance Charts: response times over time, latency distribution, percentiles, request time breakdown, throughput, errors, and virtual users.
  • AI-Powered Analysis: an interpretation of the metrics generated by Amazon Bedrock, along with validation of the numerical values referenced in the analysis.
  • Metrics Glossary: definitions of each metric, how it is calculated, an example, and why it matters.

It is important to emphasize that all metrics are calculated using Python code based on the k6 results. Amazon Bedrock is used only to interpret these values and generate the narrative analysis, with an additional validation step to verify the numerical values mentioned in the generated text.

6. Conclusions

In this article, we started with a question: how does an API behave as concurrency increases? To answer it, we implemented an automated load testing pipeline that allows us to evaluate API performance under different load scenarios and analyze the results.

This exercise allowed us to put some Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) concepts into practice: defining which aspects of the service we want to measure (SLIs), establishing what service levels we consider acceptable (SLOs), and using Grafana k6 to translate those objectives into measurable thresholds during testing.

Beyond running load tests, we also need to interpret a considerable amount of performance data. To address this, we incorporated generative AI to facilitate the analysis and generate a report that summarizes the key findings without requiring an in-depth understanding of every metric. It is important to emphasize that the metrics are calculated by code, while AI is used only to interpret them, maintaining a clear separation between the collected data and the generated conclusions.

Another important aspect is the solution's reusability. By modifying the API, queries, and load testing scenarios, we can use the same pipeline to evaluate other services. In addition, preserving the configuration and results of each execution provides traceability and facilitates future comparisons.

However, this MVP has some limitations and opportunities for improvement:

  • Geographic Coverage: tests are executed from a single AWS Region, so they do not necessarily reflect the experience of geographically distributed users.
  • Test Duration: short test scenarios may produce limited sample sizes, which can affect the stability of percentiles such as p95 and p99.
  • AI Interpretation: the analysis depends on the model and prompt used. It would be interesting to evaluate different models and refine the instructions based on the type of insights we want to obtain.
  • CI/CD Integration and Observability: the pipeline is not yet integrated into a CI/CD process. As a future improvement, we could automate testing across application versions, compare results to detect performance regressions, and incorporate Amazon CloudWatch metrics for AWS Lambda and Amazon Bedrock.

Ultimately, the goal is not simply to determine how many requests an API can handle, but to establish a reproducible process that allows us to measure its behavior, identify potential performance degradation, and evaluate how its performance evolves as we introduce changes.
