articles.title: Herding coding agents with Beads
articles.description: I am a semi-chaotic software engineer. I like to keep a bit of a pathfinder's spirit: start moving,...
articles.body_html:
I am a semi-chaotic software engineer. I like to keep a bit of a pathfinder's spirit: start moving, learn what is actually there, and fix things along the way. When I am working alone in a codebase, that can work surprisingly well. Once several coding agents are working at the same time, it gets harder to tell whether we are all heading in the same direction.

I catch myself asking the same questions: What was that agent doing? What is blocked? What is the most important thing to fix next? My usual response was to ask an agent for a fresh status update. That works, but it also spends time and tokens reconstructing a picture of the project that I had already built once.

Before Beads, I mostly asked the agent to make a plan itself. It would tell me "this will take you 2-3 weeks" and then proceed to one-shot the whole thing. I also had to give explicit instructions, and sometimes it still didn't update the docs or the progress.

Software teams solved this with issue trackers a long time ago, and Beads is that idea built for coding agents. I came across it through Steve Yegge's posts and podcast appearances. What it gave me is a way to orchestrate work across multiple chats, keep the order of the work straight, and stop depending on one agent that loses its context the day after.

What is Beads?

Beads is a command-line issue tracker for coding agents. Its command is bd. Instead of keeping a loose to-do list in a chat or a Markdown file, you create issues that can have descriptions, priorities, statuses, and relationships to other issues. Those issues persist beyond one agent conversation, so a new session can pick up the work without relying on the previous session's memory.

The useful part is the dependency graph. Suppose a feature needs a database change before the API can be updated. You record that relationship, and bd ready shows the work that has no open blockers. An agent can look at an issue, claim it, work on it, and close it. Closing a blocker makes the next task ready. The project README has the full command reference and setup.

The plan becomes part of the project workflow, instead of something I keep asking an agent to summarize.

How to start using it

You don't need a swarm of agents to get value from Beads. I installed bd, ran bd init in a project, and asked Claude to use it. Sometimes I only ran bd init and told it to use bd prime for more context.

brew install beads
cd your-project
bd init

bd init also creates or updates an AGENTS.md, so agents can find the workflow when they enter the repo. Read what it wrote and adapt it to how you want your agents to work. From there the agent runs the loop itself: bd ready to find work, bd show <id> for the details, bd update <id> --claim to take it, bd close <id> when it is done.

Here is bd ready in my Racing event tracker project, trimmed to a few rows:

$ bd ready
○ Racing_event_tracker-lj6m P1 [epic] Feeder series (F2/F3): correct calendars + session times, and guard against template rot
○ Racing_event_tracker-fwke P2 Waza follow-up: contain copilot-sdk executor + move file-shaped assertions to file/diff graders
○ Racing_event_tracker-jwt3 P2 [epic] Kiosk v2 — calm the motion, add personality
○ Racing_event_tracker-pze4 P2 [epic] Waza next plan — Track A (local, mock-only)
○ Racing_event_tracker-xdx8 P2 [bug] Stale past events linger in gold/upcoming.json

Each row is a task with no open blockers: the ID, the priority, the type in brackets when it has one, and the title.

The first real win was a bug in the data pipeline, a lingering issue. I never asked the agent to go looking for it. It spotted the problem on its own and logged an issue with the details. Beads didn't find the bug. The agent did, and Beads gave it somewhere to put it. It’s a small change, and a good place to start: let the agent file the issue instead of leaving it buried in the chat.

For bigger tasks I use a planner, or a divide-and-conquer approach. It pays off most when pieces can be picked up in parallel and I have agents to spare, either tokens or request limits. A typical plan came out at about 4 epics, depending on what I was working on, with a clear division of work between them. Sequential is the default, but subagents are where it scales. An orchestrating agent can use bd ready to hand independent tasks to subagents, and each one claims its own task with bd update <id> --claim.

What went wrong most often was issues that never got closed. The acceptance criteria included committing or asking me for a last check, the agent couldn't complete that, and the issue stayed open. I then had to close it myself or ask the agent to close it again.

The dashboard I wanted

The command line is useful for agents, but I wanted a faster way to see the whole project myself. So I built a local web dashboard for my Beads issues. It lets me scan the work, see the visual progress of subagents, add comments, and remove issues that no longer matter.

The main view is a kanban board with open, in progress and closed columns. There is also a hierarchical view, where I can edit things and watch the agents pick up work live and move it along.

I built it with Claude, in a fork of Beads, in one shot. I just told it: "build me a local dashboard so that I can view progress."

My dashboard on the Racing event tracker project: everything open, in progress and closed at a glance, updating live as the agents work.

It feels a little like project managing a team through a glorified Jira board that I built for myself. The difference is the speed: I can look at the board, spot a blocker or a questionable task, make a change, and send the agents back to work. Is this what project management feels like when the team moves this fast?

I couldn't find an existing dashboard at first. After building mine, I found the Beads community tools list and a GitHub discussion about Beads UIs. I was far from the only person who wanted a visual layer. One that looks really good to me is Beads Dashboard. It has an overview of ready, blocked and overdue work, a roadmap, and a drag-and-drop board, which is almost exactly what mine does, but as a ready-to-go VS Code extension.

So when do you build a small tool for yourself, and when do you use one that already exists? Rebuilding the same thing in several places can look wasteful from a software engineering perspective. But it took one prompt, and building it taught me more about Beads itself. For a personal tool, that was a fine trade.

The human in the loop

I used to ask an agent for a status update every time I lost the thread. Now I open the board, see what is in progress and what is stuck, and send the agents back to work. I still explore and change direction as I go, but now I do it with a map made specifically for agents, with me, the human, in the loop. Or really more of an observing human. And the question remains: how much more is there for me to observe in this abstraction layer?

This is only the start. Next, I want to explore what else Beads and agents can bring to the way I build.* *Feedback is welcome, and I'd love to hear about your own experience with Beads and agents.

References

Beads

  • Beads on GitHub, the bd issue tracker for coding agents
  • Beads documentation
  • Community tools list
  • GitHub discussion about Beads UIs

My projects

  • My Beads fork with the dashboard
  • Racing event tracker, the project where I use Beads the most

Co-written with Claude and Codex. The structure, the opening and the experience behind every story are mine. They helped fill in the gaps, tighten the sentences and check the commands against the docs.

articles.title: StartsWith Was Asking ICU Every Time
articles.description: The default StartsWith and IndexOf overloads compare text the culture-aware way, through ICU, not the literal char match you probably meant. I benchmarked the gap on two million lines and found IndexOf was the one quietly costing me.
articles.body_html:
I had an endpoint that sorts log lines as they come off a queue: route the ERROR ones one way, everything else another. The hot loop is one check, does this line start with "ERROR", and I'd written line.StartsWith("ERROR") without a second thought. It's the most obvious thing you can type.

Then I had the service under load with a profiler open, and a surprising slice of time was parked inside CompareInfo and the globalization stack underneath it. For a prefix check on ASCII log lines. That's when it clicked that StartsWith(string) doesn't do what I thought it did.

The default overload is linguistic, not literal

Here's the thing I'd forgotten. string.StartsWith(string) and string.IndexOf(string), the overloads that take only a string, don't compare characters. They compare text, using the current culture's rules, which on most boxes means routing through ICU for a full linguistic comparison. That's the machinery that knows "ﬀ" and "ff" are the same word, that a soft hyphen shouldn't count, that casing folds differently in Turkish. Handy when you're sorting names a person will read. Total overkill when you're asking whether a byte string begins with five known ASCII letters.

The fix is to say what you actually meant:

line.StartsWith("ERROR", StringComparison.Ordinal)

Ordinal means compare the char values, in order, and stop. No culture, no collation table, no ICU.

I counted it

I don't trust my gut on this stuff, so I wrote the smallest thing that would show the gap. Two million log-ish lines in an array, five prefixes mixed in so the comparison has to actually look at characters:

string[] prefixes = { "INFO ", "WARN ", "DEBUG ", "ERROR ", "TRACE " };
var lines = new string[2_000_000];
for (int i = 0; i < lines.Length; i++)
    lines[i] = prefixes[i % prefixes.Length] + "request " + i + " finished in " + (i % 400) + "ms";

Then count how many start with "ERROR", the polite way and the ordinal way:

static long CountCulture(string[] lines)
{
    long n = 0;
    foreach (string s in lines)
        if (s.StartsWith("ERROR")) n++;                       // CurrentCulture
    return n;
}

static long CountOrdinal(string[] lines)
{
    long n = 0;
    foreach (string s in lines)
        if (s.StartsWith("ERROR", StringComparison.Ordinal)) n++;
    return n;
}

The harness is nothing fancy. A stopwatch, a warmup call for each path so the JIT and the ICU tables are hot, then the best time out of seven, with the allocation counter read around each pass:

static long Measure(Action a, out long bestMs)
{
    bestMs = long.MaxValue;
    long bytes = 0;
    var sw = new Stopwatch();
    for (int run = 0; run < 7; run++)
    {
        long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        sw.Restart();
        a();
        sw.Stop();
        bytes = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() - before;
        if (sw.ElapsedMilliseconds < bestMs) bestMs = sw.ElapsedMilliseconds;
    }
    return bytes;
}

It's a single-file console app on .NET 10, top-level statements, nothing else in it. Here's what came back:

StartsWith (culture) :    27 ms
StartsWith (ordinal) :    18 ms
ratio                : 1.5x
allocated (culture)  : 0 bytes
allocated (ordinal)  : 0 bytes

That was a bit of a letdown, if I'm honest. I'd built this up in my head as the villain and it came in at 1.5x. Real, repeatable, but not the kind of number that changes your afternoon. And neither path allocates a byte, so this is pure CPU, no garbage to chase.

Then I ran the same question through IndexOf, because plenty of my "does this contain" checks are written the same lazy way:

IndexOf (culture)    :   109 ms
IndexOf (ordinal)    :    30 ms
ratio                : 3.6x

There's the one that was actually hurting. A substring search under a linguistic comparison is a lot more work than a prefix check. It can't just glance at the front, it has to weigh matches at every position with full collation rules. Roughly 3.6x on the same data. That's the call I should have been worried about from the start.

These are ratios off a Linux container, not a lab bench with the clocks pinned, so the absolute milliseconds will land somewhere else on your hardware. The shape holds up though: ordinal is cheaper, and substring search is cheaper by a lot more than a prefix check.

Ordinal isn't a free find-and-replace

Here's the caveat, and it's a real one. Ordinal and culture don't always give the same answer. That's the entire reason they're separate methods, and it's why you can't just sweep the codebase swapping one for the other.

string shy = "co­op.log";                       // a soft hyphen sits between "co" and "op"
shy.StartsWith("coop");                               // True  - culture treats the hyphen as invisible
shy.StartsWith("coop", StringComparison.Ordinal);     // False - ordinal sees the hidden char

Culture-aware comparison treats that soft hyphen as nothing, so it matches "coop". Ordinal sees nine characters and says no. For log routing, ordinal is exactly what I want: the literal content, invisible characters and all. For anything a human typed and expects to match "naturally", though, like search boxes, usernames, display sorting, the linguistic version is the correct one, and the extra cost is the price of being correct.

My rule of thumb now: if the strings are protocol rather than prose, so headers, enum names, file extensions, log levels, anything machine-generated, reach for Ordinal or OrdinalIgnoreCase by default. If a person wrote it and a person will read it, leave the culture-aware comparison where it is. The analyzer CA1310 flags exactly these call sites if you switch it on, which beats grepping for them by hand.

The quiet irony is that ordinal is both faster and usually what you meant for this kind of data. It's just not the default, and the default looks so harmless sitting there.

So what's the laziest string comparison hiding in your hot path? Check the Contains calls first, those are IndexOf underneath.

— still benchmarking corners of the standard library nobody asked me to

articles.title: Your AI Agent Isn’t Forgetting. You Might Be Feeding It Too Much.
articles.description: You paste the documentation.  Add twenty files.  Include the error logs.  Keep the entire...
articles.body_html:
You paste the documentation.

Add twenty files.

Include the error logs.

Keep the entire conversation because “the agent might need it.”

Then it misses a requirement you explained ten messages ago.

Your first reaction?

Add more instructions.

But before expanding the prompt again, look at what the agent is already reading.

More context can help. Irrelevant, repeated, or conflicting context can make the task harder.

Context overload won’t explain every mistake. Missing information, unclear requirements, and model limitations matter too. But it’s worth investigating before blaming the model—or upgrading it.

1. Context is more than your latest message

Your latest prompt might be short:

“Fix the checkout total.”

But the agent may also receive:

  • System and project instructions.
  • Earlier messages.
  • Source files.
  • Tool descriptions.
  • Search results.
  • Terminal output.
  • Summaries of previous work.

Some of that information is essential. Some may describe a problem you already solved or an approach you abandoned.

Anthropic’s context-engineering guidance emphasizes curating the information supplied throughout a task, including message history and tool results.

The practical question is:

“What does the agent need to make the next correct decision?”

2. Start with a clear task

Compare these requests:

“Check the payment system and fix anything wrong.”

And:

“Fix the calculation that allows a discount to make the order total negative. The minimum total should be zero. Preserve valid discount behavior and add a regression test.”

The second request gives the agent a specific target.

You can start with:

Goal:
Prevent negative order totals.

Expected behavior:
A discount larger than the subtotal produces a total of zero.

Scope:
Checkout calculation and relevant tests.

Verification:
Test excessive discounts and ordinary discounts.

This gives the agent a useful reference when it encounters unrelated problems.

3. Provide relevant files, then expand

For a checkout calculation bug, the agent might initially need:

  • The calculation function.
  • Its callers.
  • Relevant tests.
  • Applicable project instructions.

It probably doesn’t need the entire authentication module, deployment history, and every UI component.

Let it inspect additional files when dependencies make them relevant.

Start focused, while preserving a path to discover missing information.

Too little context can also cause mistakes. The goal is to supply useful information, not simply fewer tokens.

4. Remove instructions that are no longer true

Long conversations accumulate decisions.

You might say:

“Use library A.”

Later:

“Actually, use library B.”

Then:

“Keep the existing implementation for now.”

Without a clear update, the agent has several competing directions to interpret.

Restate the current decision:

Current decision:
Keep the existing implementation.

Superseded:
Do not proceed with the earlier library A or library B plans.

Do the same when requirements change.

A short, current description is easier to work from than a conversation full of unresolved alternatives.

5. Keep useful evidence, trim repeated output

A terminal command can produce hundreds of lines.

A search can return many near-identical results.

Those outputs may help during investigation. They don’t all need to be repeated in every progress summary.

Preserve the parts that support the next step:

  • The command that ran.
  • The relevant error.
  • The affected file or function.
  • The observed result.
  • A reference to the full log when needed.

For example:

Checkout tests:
18 passed, 1 failed.

Relevant failure:
Excessive discount returns -30 instead of 0.

Full output:
Available in the task log.

Keep the original evidence available. A summary should make it easier to find, while acknowledging anything it leaves out.

6. Write a short progress note

When a task becomes long, record its current state:

Goal:
Prevent negative checkout totals.

Completed:
Located the calculation and added a regression test.

Verified:
The new test fails on the original implementation.

Current decision:
Clamp the final total to zero.

Next:
Implement the fix and run checkout tests.

Unverified:
Browser checkout flow.

This helps a fresh session resume without reconstructing every discussion.

Check the note against the actual files and logs. A mistaken summary can carry a wrong assumption into the next session.

7. Don’t turn a fresh session into a ritual

Starting again can help when a conversation contains too much obsolete material.

But a fresh session also loses useful history.

Before restarting, prepare:

  • The current requirement.
  • Relevant file paths.
  • Decisions that still apply.
  • Verification already completed.
  • Open questions and remaining work.

Then let the agent inspect the current repository state.

A restart is useful when it improves the information available for the task. It isn’t a guaranteed fix for model mistakes.

8. Measure whether the change helps

Don’t assume a shorter context is automatically better.

Try the approach on representative tasks and compare:

  • Did the agent meet the requirements?
  • Did it miss important dependencies?
  • How many corrections were needed?
  • Did verification support the result?
  • What time and usage did the task consume?

If removing context causes missed requirements, restore the missing information.

If a concise progress note reduces repeated investigation, keep it.

Judge the workflow by the quality of the completed work.

A prompt you can reuse

Before making changes, identify the files and instructions relevant to this task. Inspect additional files when dependencies require it.

Keep a short record of the current goal, decisions, verified results, and unfinished work.

If instructions conflict or necessary information is missing, make that explicit rather than guessing.

Before you paste another file

Ask:

“What decision will this information help the agent make?”

If you have a clear answer, include it.

If it’s outdated, repetitive, or unrelated, leave it out—or make it available for retrieval instead.

A capable agent still needs a well-organized working context. Giving it useful information is part of the engineering.

Have you had better results from adding more context—or from cleaning up what was already there?

articles.title: The GUID That Sorts Itself (Until It Doesn't)
articles.description: Version 7 GUIDs give you time-ordered keys and fix the random-GUID index fragmentation problem. Then I generated 100,000 in a burst and found exactly where 'sortable' stops meaning 'ordered'.
articles.body_html:
I was looking at an index on a table whose primary key is a uniqueidentifier, and the fragmentation number was ugly. Every insert dropped a fresh Guid.NewGuid() into a random spot in the key range, so the B-tree was constantly splitting pages to make room in the middle. Classic random-GUID problem. I'd read about Version 7 GUIDs fixing this, and .NET has Guid.CreateVersion7() now, so I figured I'd swap it in and move on.

Then I got curious about how far I could actually trust the sort. So I did the thing I always do: wrote the smallest program that would tell me, and ran it instead of guessing.

What v4 keys look like when you line them up

Here's the baseline. Make six ordinary GUIDs a couple milliseconds apart, print them in the order I made them, then sort them and ask if the sorted order matches:

var v4Keys = new List<Guid>();
for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++)
{
    v4Keys.Add(Guid.NewGuid());
    Thread.Sleep(2);
}

var v4Sorted = v4Keys.OrderBy(g => g).ToList();
Console.WriteLine($"Sorted == creation order? {v4Sorted.SequenceEqual(v4Keys)}");

a23b61f1-613d-464a-a2e2-7ac3ccf522e0
ebd6f78a-afbc-42de-9450-cdee1416c9e9
3001f306-6a01-4556-b338-b3649735a280
dcf56d17-4dd3-4087-8409-9958e0e17f61
a06dcf69-ccc2-4642-b610-b21bfd05b99e
b4da4432-b310-46fc-877d-3bf6aa89de0d
Sorted == creation order? False

No surprise. A v4 GUID is 122 random bits. The value you get has nothing to do with when you asked for it, which is exactly why it scatters across the index.

v7 keys carry the time in their front teeth

A Version 7 GUID puts a 48-bit Unix-millisecond timestamp in the high bits and fills the rest with randomness. Same loop, same two-millisecond gaps, swap the factory:

var v7Keys = new List<Guid>();
for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++)
{
    v7Keys.Add(Guid.CreateVersion7());
    Thread.Sleep(2);
}

01a17719-db51-7dc3-b700-0ff42fff55da  @ 07:25:45.681
01a17719-db54-713b-adec-96911e0ab1fe  @ 07:25:45.684
01a17719-db56-7379-9292-eedae31b7e54  @ 07:25:45.686
01a17719-db58-764f-b15b-faa65bb7ff23  @ 07:25:45.688
01a17719-db5a-775e-a3b6-e12cee035baf  @ 07:25:45.690
01a17719-db5c-7722-8037-9f652b6883f6  @ 07:25:45.692
Sorted == creation order? True

Look at the left edge of each one. The prefix climbs in lockstep with the clock, so sorting the bytes sorts by time. New keys land at the end of the range instead of the middle, and that's the whole point for a database: inserts append, pages stop splitting.

And that timestamp isn't a party trick, you can read it straight back out of the key. The byte layout is big-endian for the RFC, so I ask for the bytes in that order and pull the first six:

static DateTimeOffset ReadTimestamp(Guid guid)
{
    Span<byte> bytes = stackalloc byte[16];
    guid.TryWriteBytes(bytes, bigEndian: true, out _);
    Span<byte> ms = stackalloc byte[8];
    bytes[..6].CopyTo(ms[2..]);   // 48-bit value, right-aligned in a long
    long unixMs = BinaryPrimitives.ReadInt64BigEndian(ms);
    return DateTimeOffset.FromUnixTimeMilliseconds(unixMs);
}

That bigEndian: true matters. Guid stores its first three fields in little-endian internally, so the default ToByteArray() gives you a jumbled prefix and the timestamp comes out as nonsense. The overload that takes the flag is the one you want.

The part the blog posts skip

Here's where I stopped trusting the word "sortable" and made it earn it. Those sleeps above are doing a lot of work, each key got its own millisecond. Real inserts don't wait politely. So I generated a hundred thousand of them as fast as the loop would go and asked the same question:

const int burst = 100_000;
var sameMs = new Guid[burst];
for (int i = 0; i < burst; i++)
    sameMs[i] = Guid.CreateVersion7();

var byValue = sameMs.OrderBy(g => g).ToArray();
bool matches = byValue.AsSpan().SequenceEqual(sameMs);

Burst of 100,000 v7 GUIDs took 71.8 ms
  spanned 55 distinct millisecond bucket(s)
  sorting recovers exact creation order? False

False. A hundred thousand keys fell into 55 millisecond buckets, so roughly eighteen hundred of them share each bucket, and inside a bucket the ordering bits are random. Sorting gets you to the right millisecond and then shrugs. I printed a pair to see it plainly:

Same millisecond, created a then b, but b < a byte-wise:
  a (first)  01a17719-db60-79bc-84dd-1b62234a3abb
  b (second) 01a17719-db60-753f-90e6-9be4edb208b7

Created a first, b second, same millisecond, and b sorts ahead of a. That's not a bug. .NET 10's implementation doesn't add a monotonic counter in the low bits, so two keys born in the same millisecond can come back in either order. (The spec leaves room for a counter; this runtime doesn't use one.)

This is a container, not a lab bench, and the 71.8 ms will be different on your box. The number I care about is 55 buckets, because it says the thing that matters: at insert speed, "sorted" means sorted to the millisecond, nothing finer.

So where I actually landed

For database keys, v7 is a straight upgrade over v4 and I'd reach for it by default now. The index locality is real, and getting a creation timestamp baked into the key for free is a nice bonus when you're squinting at rows in production. My one caution: don't let "time-ordered" slide into "ordered." If you need to know which of two rows was inserted first, and they might land in the same millisecond, you still need a real sequence or an identity column. The GUID won't settle that argument, and it'll look like it might, which is worse.

Want to see it on your own hardware? Here's the whole thing in one file, Program.cs, targeting net10.0 (it runs fine on .NET 9 too). No packages.

using System.Buffers.Binary;
using System.Diagnostics;

Console.WriteLine($"Running on .NET {Environment.Version}\n");

var v4Keys = new List<Guid>();
for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) { v4Keys.Add(Guid.NewGuid()); Thread.Sleep(2); }
Console.WriteLine("v4 in creation order:");
foreach (var g in v4Keys) Console.WriteLine($"  {g}");
var v4Sorted = v4Keys.OrderBy(g => g).ToList();
Console.WriteLine($"  Sorted == creation order? {v4Sorted.SequenceEqual(v4Keys)}\n");

var v7Keys = new List<Guid>();
for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) { v7Keys.Add(Guid.CreateVersion7()); Thread.Sleep(2); }
Console.WriteLine("v7 in creation order:");
foreach (var g in v7Keys) Console.WriteLine($"  {g}  @ {ReadTimestamp(g):HH:mm:ss.fff}");
var v7Sorted = v7Keys.OrderBy(g => g).ToList();
Console.WriteLine($"  Sorted == creation order? {v7Sorted.SequenceEqual(v7Keys)}\n");

const int burst = 100_000;
var sameMs = new Guid[burst];
var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
for (int i = 0; i < burst; i++) sameMs[i] = Guid.CreateVersion7();
sw.Stop();
int buckets = sameMs.Select(ReadTimestamp).Distinct().Count();
var byValue = sameMs.OrderBy(g => g).ToArray();
bool matches = byValue.AsSpan().SequenceEqual(sameMs);
Console.WriteLine($"Burst of {burst:N0} v7 GUIDs took {sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds:F1} ms");
Console.WriteLine($"  spanned {buckets} distinct millisecond bucket(s)");
Console.WriteLine($"  sorting recovers exact creation order? {matches}\n");

for (int i = 1; i < burst; i++)
{
    if (ReadTimestamp(sameMs[i]) == ReadTimestamp(sameMs[i - 1]) &&
        sameMs[i].CompareTo(sameMs[i - 1]) < 0)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Same millisecond, created a then b, but b < a byte-wise:");
        Console.WriteLine($"  a (first)  {sameMs[i - 1]}");
        Console.WriteLine($"  b (second) {sameMs[i]}");
        break;
    }
}

static DateTimeOffset ReadTimestamp(Guid guid)
{
    Span<byte> bytes = stackalloc byte[16];
    guid.TryWriteBytes(bytes, bigEndian: true, out _);
    Span<byte> ms = stackalloc byte[8];
    bytes[..6].CopyTo(ms[2..]);
    long unixMs = BinaryPrimitives.ReadInt64BigEndian(ms);
    return DateTimeOffset.FromUnixTimeMilliseconds(unixMs);
}

Have you moved any tables over to v7 keys yet, or are you still sitting on sequential integers? Curious what the fragmentation looked like before and after if you have.

— still benchmarking things nobody asked me to measure

articles.title: Getting Your First 10 Users Is Harder Than Building the Product (Or Is It?)
articles.description: TL;DR: Building proves you can create a solution. Finding users proves the solution matters to...
articles.body_html:
TL;DR: Building proves you can create a solution. Finding users proves the solution matters to someone. These are separate questions, and finishing the first never answers the second.

Reading time: about 12 minutes. For developers and first-time founders.

A developer can spend six months building a product without having to convince a single stranger to care about it.

The code either works or it doesn't. A bug can be investigated. A slow query can be measured. If a feature breaks, there's usually somewhere to start looking.

Then the product is ready, the landing page is live, and the founder starts reaching out to people.

Nothing happens.

A few people visit the website. Someone says the idea sounds interesting. A friend offers encouragement. Perhaps a handful of people create accounts, but nobody returns the following week.

Suddenly, the problem that seemed straightforward during development becomes difficult to explain. The product exists. The founder believes it solves a real problem. Yet the people who supposedly need it aren't showing up.

This is where a familiar piece of startup advice enters the conversation: getting your first ten users is harder than building the product.

There is a reason the advice resonates, especially with developers who are building their first businesses. But it also leaves an important question unanswered.

The real question

Is finding those first ten users actually harder than building the product, or does it feel harder because founders have less control over what happens next?

The distinction matters. If you misunderstand why people aren't using your product, you can spend months trying to solve the wrong problem.

Jump to a section
  1. Building gives you feedback. Selling gives you silence.
  2. Stripe's early customers didn't arrive through a signup page
  3. Ten signups can still mean zero real users
  4. When the advice is right, and when it isn't
  5. A quiet launch can mean four different things
  6. What should you actually do to find the first ten?
  7. The first ten are not the finish line

1. Building gives you feedback. Selling gives you silence.

Consider what happens when a developer encounters a difficult technical problem.

The solution might take hours, days, or even weeks. But there is usually a way to investigate it. You can inspect the logs, reproduce the failure, test a different approach, and gradually narrow down the possibilities.

Progress isn't guaranteed, but the work often produces information you can use.

Customer acquisition is different.

You send twenty carefully written messages and receive two replies. You publish a detailed explanation of your product and nobody clicks through. You demonstrate a feature to someone who says they would love to use it, then never hear from them again.

You have an outcome, but you don't necessarily know what caused it.

Perhaps the people you contacted don't have the problem. Perhaps they do, but your message arrived at the wrong time. Perhaps the product is useful but switching to it would take too much effort. Perhaps they simply don't trust an unfamiliar founder with something important to their work.

Those explanations require different responses. Silence alone cannot tell you which one is correct.

This is one reason acquisition can feel more frustrating than development. With code, you can often make the next experiment more specific because you understand the system you're investigating. With customers, you are still learning how the system works.

You are learning what people care about, what they already use, what they will pay to change, and what makes them trust a product they have never tried.

And you are learning all of this while trying to persuade them to give you their time.

That is a genuinely difficult problem. But it isn't necessarily a harder problem in every measurable sense. A technically ambitious product might require years of engineering, while a simple product could find its first customers in a few days.

The more useful distinction:

Building tests... Finding customers tests...
The question Can you create the solution? Does the solution matter enough that someone will act on it?
Feedback you get Logs, errors, measurable results Often silence
Who controls the outcome Mostly you Mostly other people

Those are separate questions, and finishing the first does not answer the second.

2. Stripe's early customers didn't arrive through a signup page

In his 2013 essay Do Things That Don't Scale, Paul Graham describes how Patrick and John Collison acquired early users for Stripe.1

When somebody agreed to try the payment integration, the brothers wouldn't simply send a link and wait. They would ask to borrow the person's laptop and help install it immediately.

Y Combinator came to call this the "Collison installation."

The approach seems almost excessive now. Why should a founder personally install a product when the whole point of software is to make the experience repeatable?

Because the founders were solving a problem that a signup page couldn't solve for them.

A person who agrees to try a product has made a relatively inexpensive commitment. They can change their mind without consequence. Actually installing it requires more effort and brings the product into contact with the person's real workflow.

By helping with the installation, the founders removed friction and discovered what happened when someone tried to use Stripe for real.

Context matters. Stripe was addressing a concrete problem for developers and businesses, and its early founders had access to a network of potential customers through the startup ecosystem. Their approach does not prove that every product can acquire customers by offering personal onboarding.

It does show something more practical: sometimes the obstacle between interest and usage is not a lack of awareness. It is the work required to get started.

What that looks like in practice:

  • Developer tool: help someone integrate it
  • Software for accountants: import a customer's existing data
  • A service: deliver the first result personally before asking for a longer commitment

These approaches do not scale indefinitely. That is precisely why they can be valuable at the beginning.

Before automating an onboarding process, a founder needs to understand where people struggle with it. Before spending heavily on marketing, they need to know what happens after somebody responds.

The first ten customers can be valuable for the revenue they bring in. They can also reveal problems that a founder working alone would never have discovered.

3. Ten signups can still mean zero real users

There is another problem with the way founders talk about their first users: the word user can describe several very different situations.

  1. Someone visits the landing page.
  2. Someone else joins the waitlist.
  3. A third person creates an account, opens the dashboard, and leaves.

All three might appear in a growth report. None necessarily demonstrates that the product is delivering its promised value.

This distinction is more than a matter of terminology.

In his account of Superhuman's product-market-fit process, founder Rahul Vohra described a company that had spent years building its email product but still needed a clearer way to measure whether users genuinely valued it.2

Superhuman surveyed people who had used the product at least twice in the preceding two weeks. It asked how they would feel if they could no longer use it.

Only 22% said they would be very disappointed.

That result mattered because these weren't simply people who had heard about Superhuman. They had already experienced the product. Yet most did not consider it indispensable.

The team used the survey responses to identify the people who valued the product most, understand what those people appreciated, and make improvements intended to strengthen product-market fit. Vohra subsequently reported that the score rose from 22% to 58%.

- 22%  "very disappointed"  (before)
+ 58%  "very disappointed"  (after)

58%−22%=36 percentage points 58\% - 22\% = 36 \text{ percentage points} 58%−22%=36 percentage points

What this example does and doesn't establish

There are limits to what this example establishes. The survey is a useful diagnostic, not a universal scientific test that can independently prove product-market fit. The results came from Superhuman's particular audience and product, and a high score does not guarantee a sustainable business.

Still, the underlying problem is important.

Getting somebody to sign up and getting somebody to care whether your product disappears are not the same achievement.

For a founder trying to find ten users, this means the milestone needs a definition.

Ten registered accounts might be an appropriate early milestone for testing whether people will respond to an offer. Ten people who repeatedly use a core feature tell you something different. Ten paying customers tell you something different again.

None of those numbers is automatically the right target. The right target depends on what the product is supposed to accomplish.

Product type A meaningful signal might be
Tool used every morning Returning frequently
Quarterly accounting software Completing the quarterly task (daily usage would be a strange expectation)
One-time service Successful completion and willingness to recommend the provider

A founder should measure the behaviour that demonstrates value, rather than assume every product needs the same pattern of engagement.

Read the Superhuman product-market-fit story

4. When the advice is right, and when it isn't

The claim that customer acquisition is harder than building is most convincing when a founder has a working product but no reliable way to reach people who need it.

Imagine a developer who builds a scheduling tool for freelance designers. The technical work is manageable. The product works. But the developer has no existing audience among designers, no relationships with design agencies, and no idea where these freelancers look for tools.

The product might be finished in a month. Finding a group of people willing to try it, learning what they actually need, and discovering whether any of them will pay could take much longer.

The developer isn't necessarily struggling because the product is bad. They are trying to solve a problem for a group of people they don't yet understand well enough.

Now consider a different founder: an accountant who builds a small tool to automate a tedious task that several existing clients already complain about. The founder knows the workflow, has access to the intended users, and can test the tool with people who experience the problem every week.

The technical challenge could be the hardest part of that business. Finding the first few users might be comparatively straightforward.

Developer building for designers Accountant building for own clients
Existing audience No Yes
Knows the workflow No Yes
Likely hardest part Finding users Building the tool

Neither example is unusual enough to support a universal rule. Together, they show why the headline depends on the founder, the market, and the product.

Existing distribution changes the equation, too. Someone with an established audience, a respected reputation in a niche, or a network of potential buyers isn't starting from the same position as someone nobody knows.

That advantage is real. It doesn't mean their product is better, or that their acquisition strategy is automatically repeatable. It means some of the work required to earn attention happened before the product was launched.

The same qualification applies to technically novel products. If a founder doesn't yet know whether a proposed system can work at an acceptable cost, speed, or level of reliability, engineering experiments may need to come first. Talking to potential customers cannot resolve every question about technical feasibility.

The mistake is treating either building or customer acquisition as the correct first step for every startup.

Sometimes the founder needs to write more code. Sometimes they need to speak to potential customers before writing another line. Often, they need to do both, using what they learn from one to inform the other.

5. A quiet launch can mean four different things

Suppose you launch your product and, after several weeks, you still haven't found ten meaningful users.

The tempting response is to do more marketing. Post in more communities. Send more messages. Try another launch platform.

That might help. But first, consider where the process is breaking.

flowchart LR
    A[Launch] --> B{Right people<br/>seeing it?}
    B -- No --> C[1. Reach problem]
    B -- Yes --> D{Taking the<br/>next step?}
    D -- No --> E[2. Offer problem]
    D -- Yes --> F{Reaching the<br/>main benefit?}
    F -- No --> G[3. Activation problem]
    F -- Yes --> H{Returning<br/>or paying?}
    H -- No --> I[4. Retention problem]
    H -- Yes --> J[Keep going]

1. The right people aren't seeing the product

Perhaps the product solves a genuine problem, but your potential customers don't spend time on the channels you're using. Or perhaps you're targeting such a broad audience that your message never feels relevant to anyone in particular.

In this case, changing the product may accomplish very little. You need to understand where the intended customers already look for solutions and how to reach them.

2. People see the product but don't take the next step

This could mean the value proposition is unclear. It could also mean the problem isn't urgent, the price is too high, the proposed solution feels risky, or the person reading your message doesn't have the authority to make a purchase.

It is worth asking what your offer requires someone to believe before they act. An unfamiliar product asking for access to sensitive business data has a much larger trust problem than a free tool that works entirely in the browser.

3. People try the product but never reach its main benefit

Perhaps setup takes too long. Maybe the first screen asks users to configure five things before they can accomplish anything useful. The product might even work exactly as intended, but the value isn't apparent to a new user.

This is where watching someone use the product can reveal more than another round of promotional posts.

4. People get value once but don't return or pay

This is the most uncomfortable possibility because the founder has evidence that the product can work for someone, yet the behaviour isn't continuing.

The problem might be retention, pricing, a low-frequency need, or a mismatch between the person using the product and the person expected to pay. It could also mean the product is useful but not important enough to replace an existing habit.

Not a complete diagnosis. These four categories aren't exhaustive, and the boundaries between them aren't always clean. A confusing product can look like a marketing problem. A weak offer can look like a distribution problem. Low retention can reflect a product that works perfectly but solves a problem people rarely encounter.

The point is not to label every failure immediately.

It is to stop treating every failure as the same failure.

6. What should you actually do to find the first ten?

The best starting point is smaller than a launch campaign.

Choose a specific group of people who already experience the problem your product is intended to solve. Be precise enough that you can identify actual individuals, rather than an enormous category of potential customers.

Then investigate what they do today.

If you're building invoice software for freelancers, find out how those freelancers currently create invoices, follow up on unpaid bills, and keep track of their income. Ask what happens when the process goes wrong. Look for examples of real frustration, time lost, money lost, or workarounds people have already built.

Steve Blank's writing on customer development makes a useful distinction here: founders begin with hypotheses about customers and their needs, then test those hypotheses through conversations and experiments.3 The goal is to discover what is true, not simply to collect encouraging responses.

That means asking about actual behaviour is usually more informative than asking whether somebody likes your idea.

Example: weak evidence vs. strong evidence

A person may tell you they would happily use an invoicing tool. That costs them nothing.

Finding out what they currently use, whether they have paid for alternatives, and whether they'll try your product with a real invoice gives you stronger evidence.

Once you understand the problem, offer a small, concrete next step.

Don't necessarily ask someone to adopt your entire product. Ask whether they'll try one feature, bring one real task into it, or spend twenty minutes showing you how they currently handle the problem.

If the product is ready, help them use it. If it isn't, a prototype or a manually delivered version of the service might be enough to test the underlying assumption, provided you don't misrepresent what you've built.

Track what happens next

Stage What to record
Reached Did the intended person actually see the offer?
Responded Did they reply or ask a meaningful question?
Tried Did they attempt the real task?
Activated Did they reach the product's core value?
Returned Did they use it again when the need arose?
Committed Did they pay, renew, recommend it, or make another meaningful commitment?

Not every product needs all six stages, and not every commitment looks like a payment. The table is a way to make the process observable, not a universal funnel that every business must follow.

Keep notes on why people stop, preferably in their own words. A polite refusal and a detailed objection are not equivalent. Neither is the same as someone who tries the product, gets value from it, and simply doesn't need it again until next month.

Then choose the next experiment based on what you learned:

  • [ ] The wrong people are seeing the offer: change the audience or channel
  • [ ] The right people understand the offer but don't care enough to try it: investigate the problem and the value proposition
  • [ ] They try the product but fail to reach its main benefit: work on that experience
  • [ ] They get value but don't return or pay: investigate the frequency, importance, and economics of the problem

Two weeks can be enough to uncover useful patterns when the target customers are accessible and the product delivers value quickly. It may be nowhere near enough for a business with a long sales cycle or a problem that occurs only a few times a year.

The objective isn't to promise ten users within fourteen days. It is to finish the experiment knowing more than you did when you started.

7. The first ten are not the finish line

There is a reason founders remember their first users. Each one represents a decision that happened outside the codebase: somebody noticed the product, considered it relevant, decided to try it, and perhaps found enough value to return.

But the number ten can be misleading.

Ten users who... ...might tell you
signed up because a friend asked Very little about whether strangers will pay
independently share the same painful problem and pay to solve it A great deal
never return A product problem that another hundred signups would only make harder to ignore

The work isn't finished when the tenth person arrives. That's often when the next question becomes possible.

  • Can you find another ten people with the same problem?
  • Can you reach them through a process you understand?
  • Do they experience enough value to keep using the product?
  • Does acquiring and serving them make economic sense?

Those questions are harder to answer than whether a product can attract ten signups, and they matter more to the future of the business.

So, is getting your first ten users harder than building the product?

Sometimes. Especially when the founder understands the technology but knows very little about the people who might buy it. But the comparison becomes less useful when it turns into a universal rule, or when it encourages founders to treat engineering and customer discovery as competing activities.

A product can be technically excellent and commercially irrelevant. It can also be commercially promising before its engineering is finished. The difficult work is finding out which situation you're in while there is still time to change direction.

That begins with a more useful question than how to get ten users.

Your next question

What would you need to learn from the next person who tries your product to know what to do next?

Share your answer in the comments.

The Startup Café — Real Startup Lessons. Beyond the Hype.

  1. Paul Graham, "Do Things That Don't Scale," 2013. The essay is where the Collison installation story comes from. ↩

  2. Rahul Vohra's account on the First Round Review. The 22% and 58% figures come from Superhuman's own survey of its own users, so treat them as one company's data point. ↩

  3. Steve Blank's customer development writing is a collection of posts, so start with the ones on customer discovery and hypothesis testing. ↩

articles.title: My VS Code setup went from 47 extensions to 6. My productivity went up.
articles.description: I counted my VS Code extensions. There were 47. My editor took 8 seconds to start, lagged when I...
articles.body_html:
I counted my VS Code extensions. There were 47. My editor took 8 seconds to start, lagged when I typed, and crashed once a week. I disabled 41 of them and kept 6. Here is what happened.

The problem

Extension creep is gradual. You install a formatter, then a linter, then a theme, then a snippet pack, then a language support extension for a framework you tried once and never used again. Each one seems small. Each one adds startup time, memory usage, and editor complexity.

My 47 extensions included:

  • 5 formatters (Prettier, ESLint, Stylelint, Beautify, Rustfmt)
  • 4 language packs (Python, Go, Rust, Java, only Python was active)
  • 3 themes (one in use, two installed "to try later")
  • 6 snippet packs (React, Vue, Python, Docker, Git, and a generic HTML one)
  • 4 Git extensions (GitLens, Git Graph, GitHub Pull Requests, Git History)
  • 3 AI extensions (GitHub Copilot, Codeium, Tabnine, all disabled in favor of Cursor)
  • 22 others (Docker, YAML, TOML, markdown preview, CSV viewer, path intellisense, import cost, indent rainbow, bracket pair colorizer, and more)

Most of these I had installed once and forgotten about. They were running on every startup, consuming memory, registering commands, and contributing to the status bar.

What I kept

I went through each extension and asked: "Have I used this in the last week?" If the answer was no, I disabled it. Here is what survived:

1. Prettier. Code formatting. I use it on every file. Non-negotiable.

2. ESLint. Linting. Same as Prettier, I use it constantly. The two work together.

3. GitLens. I use the blame and diff features daily. The rest of GitLens (code lens, file history, commit search) I could live without, but the blame view alone justifies the extension.

4. Astro. Language support for Astro, which is my primary framework. Without it, .astro files are unstyled HTML.

5. Tailwind CSS IntelliSense. Autocomplete for Tailwind classes. I write Tailwind every day. Without this, I am guessing at class names.

6. Error Lens. Shows errors and warnings inline instead of requiring a hover. It is a small UX improvement that saves me hundreds of micro-interactions per day.

That is it. Six extensions.

What happened

Startup time: 8 seconds to 1.5 seconds. The difference is immediately noticeable. I open and close the editor many times a day, and the 6.5 second saving compounds.

Memory usage: 1.2 GB to 380 MB. VS Code went from being the heaviest application on my machine to being lighter than my browser. The lag when typing in large files disappeared.

Crashes: once a week to zero in six weeks. I cannot prove causation, but the correlation is strong. Extension conflicts are a known cause of VS Code instability, and removing 41 of them eliminated a lot of potential conflicts.

Productivity: up, measurably. I was spending time managing extensions: updating them, configuring them, disabling ones that conflicted, and debugging issues caused by interaction between them. That time is gone. The editor does what I need and gets out of the way.

What I learned about extension creep

Extensions are not free. Each one adds to startup time, memory footprint, and editor complexity. The cost is invisible until you remove them and feel the difference.

You do not use most of your extensions. 41 out of 47 had not been used in the last week. Some had not been used in months. They were running anyway.

The best extensions are the ones you forget you have. Prettier, ESLint, Error Lens: these work silently. They do not have popups, side panels, or status bar clutter. They do their job and disappear.

AI extensions are redundant when you use an AI editor. I was running Copilot, Codeium, and Tabnine inside VS Code while also using Cursor (which has its own AI). The AI extensions were disabled but still loaded. Removing them freed memory and removed a source of confusion about which AI was active.

The 2026 editor landscape

The choice in 2026 is not "which extensions should I install." It is "which editor should I use." The landscape:

  • VS Code remains the default. The extension ecosystem is the largest. With a minimal setup, it is fast and reliable.
  • Cursor is VS Code with AI built in. If you are paying for an AI assistant, Cursor replaces the need for AI extensions.
  • Zed is the performance option. Rust-native, fast startup, built-in collaboration. Smaller extension ecosystem.
  • JetBrains (WebStorm, IntelliJ) is the heavy option. Built-in tooling for everything, but higher memory footprint and per-seat licensing.

My current setup is Cursor (which is VS Code under the hood) with the same 6 extensions. The AI features are built into the editor, so I do not need AI extensions. The 6 extensions I kept are the ones that do work the AI cannot do: format my code, lint it, show Astro syntax, autocomplete Tailwind classes, and display errors inline.

If you want to try this

  1. Open your extensions tab. Sort by "installed."
  2. For each extension, ask: "Have I used this in the last week?"
  3. Disable everything where the answer is no. Do not uninstall yet, just disable.
  4. Work for a week. If you need an extension you disabled, re-enable it.
  5. After a week, uninstall everything that is still disabled.
  6. Measure your startup time before and after. The difference is your motivation to keep it lean.

The temptation to install will return. Every blog post about "10 VS Code extensions you must have" will add to your list. The discipline is not "never install." It is "install, try, and remove if you do not use it within a week."

articles.title: JSON.parse Source Text Access: Stop Losing Precision on Big IDs
articles.description: JSON.parse can now hand your reviver the original source text of every number, and JSON.rawJSON lets you write it back out exactly. Here's how to round-trip 64-bit IDs and decimals without string hacks.
articles.body_html:
Your API returns an order ID of 9007199254740993. Your frontend logs 9007199254740992. Nobody touched it. JSON.parse quietly rounded it, because every JSON number becomes a JavaScript double, and doubles only hold integers exactly up to Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (9007199254740991). Anything bigger gets snapped to the nearest representable value before your code ever sees it.

The usual workarounds are all a little sad. Ask the backend to send IDs as strings (id_str, if you remember the old Twitter API). Pull in a third-party parser like json-bigint. Or run a regex over the raw response to wrap long numbers in quotes before parsing, and hope nothing in a string field looks like a number. The platform now has a real fix: the JSON.parse source text access proposal, which adds a context argument to revivers and a matching JSON.rawJSON() for serialization. It reached Stage 4 at TC39 in late 2025, and it is already Baseline: Chrome 114, Firefox 135, Safari 18.4, Node 21, Deno 1.33, and Bun 1.1.43 all ship it.

The reviver gets a third argument

A reviver has always received (key, value). It now receives (key, value, context), and for primitive values context.source is the exact slice of JSON text that produced value. The number was still parsed into a lossy double, but you get the original digits next to it, so you can decide what it should become.

const json = '{"orderId": 9007199254740993, "total": 42.5}';

const order = JSON.parse(json, (key, value, context) => {
  if (key === "orderId") {
    // value is already rounded; context.source is not
    return BigInt(context.source);
  }
  return value;
});

order.orderId; // 9007199254740993n
order.total; // 42.5

Keying off property names works when you control the schema, but a generic version is more useful in a shared fetch helper. Promote only integers that actually lost precision, and leave everything else alone:

const INTEGER = /^-?\d+$/;

export function preciseReviver(key, value, context) {
  if (
    typeof value === "number" &&
    !Number.isSafeInteger(value) &&
    context?.source &&
    INTEGER.test(context.source)
  ) {
    return BigInt(context.source);
  }
  return value;
}

const res = await fetch("/api/orders");
const data = JSON.parse(await res.text(), preciseReviver);

Two details there matter. Response.json() doesn't accept a reviver, so you read the body as text and parse it yourself. And the optional chaining on context?.source is deliberate: context.source only exists for primitives. When the reviver is called for an object or array, source is absent, because there's no single meaningful slice of text to give you once the children have already been revived.

Writing it back out with JSON.rawJSON

Parsing is half the problem. Hand that BigInt to JSON.stringify and you get TypeError: Do not know how to serialize a BigInt. Convert it to a Number first and you're back to rounding. JSON.rawJSON() closes the loop: it wraps a piece of JSON text that stringify will emit verbatim.

function preciseReplacer(key, value) {
  return typeof value === "bigint" ? JSON.rawJSON(value.toString()) : value;
}

JSON.stringify({ orderId: 9007199254740993n }, preciseReplacer);
// '{"orderId":9007199254740993}'

The output is a real JSON number, not a quoted string, so a Go or Java backend expecting an int64 reads it without any schema change. JSON.rawJSON is strict about what it accepts: the text must be valid JSON for a primitive, so JSON.rawJSON('[1, 2]') or a string containing a raw line break throws a SyntaxError. The returned object is frozen with a null prototype, and JSON.isRawJSON() tells you if you're holding one.

Decimals, not just big integers

Money is the other place this pays off. 0.1 parsed as a double is not exactly one tenth, and a payments API that returns "amount": 19.99 hands you a value that's already slightly wrong before your decimal library sees it. With context.source you can feed the original digits straight into whatever arbitrary-precision type you use:

import Decimal from "decimal.js";

const invoice = JSON.parse(body, (key, value, context) =>
  key === "amount" ? new Decimal(context.source) : value,
);

On the way out, JSON.rawJSON(amount.toFixed(2)) writes 19.99 as an unquoted number again.

When not to reach for it

A reviver runs once per value in the document, so it is measurably slower than a plain JSON.parse on large payloads. If your IDs are already strings, or every number fits in the safe range, you don't need any of this. In TypeScript, older lib definitions may not know about the third reviver argument or JSON.rawJSON yet, so you might need a small ambient declaration until your lib setting catches up. For older browsers, core-js ships a polyfill for both halves.

The bigger change is where the fix lives. Precision used to be something you negotiated with the backend team or patched with a dependency. Now it's a few lines in the one fetch helper every request already goes through. MDN's pages on JSON.parse() and JSON.rawJSON() have the full reference, and the TC39 proposal covers the design reasoning.

articles.title: From zero to your first Garmin data in Node
articles.description: Sign in to Garmin Connect from Node with garminconnect-js, handle MFA, keep the session, and print last night's sleep and HRV. Part 1 of Build with Garmin data.
articles.body_html:
For developers. Just want to ask Claude about your training, with no code? Start with Your Garmin data in Claude instead.

In my first post I introduced garminconnect-js, a typed, zero-dependency Garmin Connect client for Node. This series is the hands-on version: four posts that take you from an empty folder to an app that reads and writes Garmin data.

This first part covers the foundation everything else stands on:

  1. Signing in, including two-factor (MFA) codes
  2. Keeping the session, so you sign in once and not on every run
  3. Reading data, and what "no data" looks like
  4. Handling errors properly

By the end you'll have a small command-line script that prints last night's sleep and HRV.

Written against garminconnect-js 0.10.0. Every snippet here type-checks against that version.

What you need

  • Node 18 or newer (node --version)
  • A Garmin Connect account with some data in it. A watch that records sleep makes this post more fun, but everything works without one.

A quick note on what this library is: Garmin has no public API for your own Connect data, so garminconnect-js talks to the same endpoints Garmin's web and mobile apps use. It's unofficial, those endpoints can change, and it's server-side only. Your Garmin password and tokens should never reach a browser.

Set up the project 

mkdir garmin-sleep && cd garmin-sleep
npm init -y
npm install garminconnect-js
npm install -D tsx typescript @types/node

On Deno or Bun, the same code is published on JSR as @dynamicsninja/garminconnect (npx jsr add @dynamicsninja/garminconnect).

tsx runs TypeScript files directly, so there's no build step for a script like this. Add "type": "module" to package.json so top-level await works:

{
  "type": "module"
}

And keep your secrets out of git from the start:

echo "tokens/" >> .gitignore
echo ".env" >> .gitignore

Step 1: sign in once

Create login.ts:

import { createInterface } from "node:readline/promises";
import { stdin, stdout } from "node:process";
import { GarminClient, FileTokenStore } from "garminconnect-js";

const client = new GarminClient({ tokenStore: new FileTokenStore("./tokens") });

const result = await client.login(process.env.GARMIN_EMAIL!, process.env.GARMIN_PASSWORD!);

if (result.state === "mfa_required") {
  const rl = createInterface({ input: stdin, output: stdout });
  const code = await rl.question("Garmin sent you a code. Enter it: ");
  rl.close();
  await client.resumeLogin(result.mfaState, code.trim());
}

console.log("Signed in. Your session is saved in ./tokens");

Run it with your credentials in the environment:

GARMIN_EMAIL=you@example.com GARMIN_PASSWORD='...' npx tsx login.ts

(On Windows PowerShell, set them first with $env:GARMIN_EMAIL="you@example.com", or use a .env file and node --env-file=.env --import tsx login.ts.)

If you use a .env file and your password contains a #, put the value in quotes: GARMIN_PASSWORD="...". Without them, Node reads everything from the # on as a comment, Garmin gets a shortened password, and you get a GarminAuthError that looks like a wrong password. It happened to me while testing this post.

Three things are worth understanding here.

login() doesn't throw or block on MFA. If your account has two-factor turned on, it returns { state: "mfa_required", mfaState } and you finish with resumeLogin(mfaState, code). In a script, that's a prompt. In a web app, the two halves can happen in two separate HTTP requests, which is exactly what Part 2 builds on.

FileTokenStore keeps your session on disk. After a successful login, the library writes two small JSON files to ./tokens. Those files are your Garmin session, so treat them like a password: keep them out of git, and off any machine you don't trust.

Sign in as rarely as possible. Garmin rate-limits sign-ins, sometimes after only one or two attempts in a row. The library already falls back to Garmin's web sign-in when the mobile one is rate-limited, but the real fix is not to sign in repeatedly. Sign in once, then reuse the tokens.

Step 2: reuse the session

Every other script starts like this instead:

import { GarminClient, Garmin, FileTokenStore } from "garminconnect-js";

const client = new GarminClient({ tokenStore: new FileTokenStore("./tokens") });

if (!(await client.loadTokens())) {
  console.error("Not signed in yet. Run login.ts first.");
  process.exit(1);
}

const garmin = new Garmin(client);

loadTokens() returns false rather than throwing when there's nothing saved, so the "not signed in" case is just an if.

You never refresh tokens yourself. The short-lived access token lasts about a day, and the library renews it automatically before any request that needs it, then saves the new one back through your token store. The underlying session keeps rolling forward as long as you make a call at least once every 30 days. Go longer than that and you'll get a GarminAuthError, which means "sign in again".

Garmin is the class with all the methods (about 200 of them). Create one per signed-in user and reuse it: it caches your profile, which most date-based calls need.

Step 3: read last night's sleep

Here's the full script, sleep.ts:

import { GarminClient, Garmin, FileTokenStore, GarminAuthError, GarminError } from "garminconnect-js";
import type { PersonalApi } from "garminconnect-js";

const client = new GarminClient({ tokenStore: new FileTokenStore("./tokens") });
if (!(await client.loadTokens())) {
  console.error("Not signed in yet. Run login.ts first.");
  process.exit(1);
}
const garmin = new Garmin(client);

// Garmin files a night's sleep under the date you woke up.
const date = process.argv[2] ?? new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10);

const hours = (seconds?: number | null) =>
  seconds == null ? "?" : `${Math.floor(seconds / 3600)}h ${Math.round((seconds % 3600) / 60)}m`;

try {
  const [sleep, hrv] = await Promise.all([garmin.getSleepData(date), garmin.getHrvData(date)]);

  const night = sleep?.dailySleepDTO as PersonalApi.DailySleepDTO | undefined;
  if (!night?.sleepTimeSeconds) {
    console.log(`No sleep recorded for ${date}.`);
  } else {
    console.log(`Sleep on ${date}: ${hours(night.sleepTimeSeconds)}`);
    console.log(`  Score: ${night.sleepScores?.overall?.value ?? "n/a"}`);
    console.log(`  Deep ${hours(night.deepSleepSeconds)}, REM ${hours(night.remSleepSeconds)}`);
  }

  const summary = hrv?.hrvSummary;
  if (summary) {
    console.log(`HRV: ${summary.lastNightAvg ?? "?"} ms last night, ${summary.weeklyAvg ?? "?"} ms weekly average (${summary.status ?? "no status"})`);
  }
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof GarminAuthError) {
    console.error("Your Garmin session has expired. Run login.ts again.");
  } else if (error instanceof GarminError) {
    console.error(`Garmin error: ${error.message}`);
  } else {
    throw error;
  }
  process.exit(1);
}

Run it for today, or for any date:

npx tsx sleep.ts
npx tsx sleep.ts 2026-10-20

The output looks like this (your numbers will differ):

Sleep on 2026-10-20: 7h 34m
  Score: 81
  Deep 1h 22m, REM 1h 51m
HRV: 52 ms last night, 49 ms weekly average (BALANCED)

"No data" is not an error

Notice the checks for null and undefined. For most Garmin endpoints, an empty answer is normal: no watch worn that night, no HRV feature on your device, or simply a date before you owned the watch. getSleepData and getHrvData return null in that case; they don't throw.

A few methods do throw on an empty answer, for example getActivity when the id doesn't exist. The library's reference says which is which, method by method, so check there rather than assuming one rule for all.

Dates are UTC calendar dates

Every method takes a date either as "YYYY-MM-DD" or as a Date. A Date is converted with toISOString(), which is UTC. If you're in New York and pass new Date() at 9 p.m., you're asking for tomorrow. When the day matters, pass the string you mean.

Typed, but honest about it

Most responses have real types. Many are generated from Garmin's own Personal API spec and exported as PersonalApi.*, which is where DailySleepDTO above comes from. A few raw responses are deliberately loose (Record<string, unknown>) because Garmin's shape varies too much to promise more. That's why the script narrows dailySleepDTO to the spec's type in one place.

Handling errors

Every error the library throws is a GarminError or a subclass, so you can handle them by type:

Error Means What to do
GarminAuthError The session is gone or invalid (401/403, expired tokens) Sign in again
GarminRateLimitError Garmin said 429 Back off. It carries retryAfter (seconds) when Garmin sends one
GarminConnectionError Network failure or timeout, after retries Retry later, but read the note below
GarminHttpError Any other non-2xx Inspect status and body

The library already retries GET requests on network errors and 5xx responses, with backoff. It never retries a POST, so a write can't be duplicated behind your back.

One trap: a few permanent errors are deliberately reported as GarminConnectionError, such as uploading an activity that already exists. So never write a blind catch (e) { if (e instanceof GarminConnectionError) retryForever() }. Look at the message, or at error.cause, first.

Beyond sleep

The same pattern, sign in once and then call methods, covers the rest of your data. A few to try in the same script:

await garmin.getUserSummary(date);            // steps, calories, stress, Body Battery for one day
await garmin.getDailySummaries("2026-10-01", "2026-10-20"); // the same, one row per day, for a range
await garmin.getTrainingReadiness(date);      // readiness score and what's driving it
await garmin.getRacePredictions();            // 5K, 10K, half and full marathon predictions
await garmin.getActivities(0, 5);             // your five most recent activities

And if you need an endpoint the library doesn't wrap, client.connectapi(path) calls any Garmin Connect path with the same authentication. You'll see that in Part 4.

What's next

You now have the two building blocks: a session you sign in to once, and typed reads with proper error handling. In Part 2 we'll put this behind a web app: a Next.js app where users sign in with their own Garmin account (MFA included, across two requests), with tokens stored in your database instead of a folder.

  • Docs and every method: garmin.ficdev.xyz
  • Source (MIT): github.com/DynamicsNinja/garminconnect-js

If something here doesn't match what your account returns, tell me in the comments. Undocumented endpoints are full of surprises, and every report makes the library better.
